articles.title_orig: China posts biggest monthly gold reserve increase in 3 years
articles.title_zh: China posts biggest monthly gold reserve increase in 3 years
articles.content_orig:
China's central bank stepped up its gold purchases as prices fell in September, recording the biggest monthly increase in its official gold reserves in three years, official data showed on Wednesday.
The country's gold reserves rose by 740,000 ounces to 77.47 million ounces as of the end of September, marking the 23rd consecutive month of purchases, according to the People's Bank of China.
The latest increase was the largest since September 2023, when reserves rose by 840,000 ounces, according to market tracker Wind Info. It also exceeded the increases of 650,000 ounces in August and 640,000 ounces in July.
Meanwhile, China's foreign exchange reserves stood at $3.4 trillion at the end of September, down $38.1 billion, or 1.11 percent, from a month earlier, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange said.
ALSO READ: China reports slight increase in gold consumption
SAFE attributed the decline to the combined effects of currency translation and changes in asset prices, as the US dollar index rose and prices of major global financial assets generally fell during the month.
China's economy remained broadly stable, with new growth drivers gaining strength, supporting the overall stability of foreign exchange reserves, SAFE said.

articles.title_orig: Standing with young workers on World Day for Decent Work
articles.title_zh: Standing with young workers on World Day for Decent Work
articles.content_orig:
This year, the World Day for Decent Work on 7 October centres on young workers’ demands for respect, rights, secure work and a wage they can live off. To mark the day, we spoke to UNI Youth Global President Crisnalda Nhamucale , a member of our commerce affiliate SINECOSSE in Mozambique. She told us about the challenges facing young workers and what unions and governments must do to build a fairer future of work.
This interview has been translated from Portuguese.
What does decent work mean to you personally, and what does it mean for the young workers you represent? Decent work means any work carried out between worker and employer in which fundamental rights at work are respected, women and men are treated equally and social dialogue is prioritized. Work is only decent when wages and social conditions are fair and workers’ safety is guaranteed. For young people, decent work goes beyond wages and occupational health and safety. To me, work is dignified or decent when it gives young people ongoing training and professional recognition.
Young people around the world are working in very different contexts, from retail and finance to call centres and platform work. Despite these differences, what common concerns do you hear from young UNI members across regions?
Technology may be changing fast, but young people’s biggest concern hasn’t changed. The most pressing challenge of all is still getting a job in the first place.
As technology and artificial intelligence change the world of work, platform work has become a major source of jobs for young people. What protections do they need, and what must change to make platform work decent work?
For young people, the biggest danger in platform work is the lack of protection, because it is a relationship without the traditional employment contract. Suppose they were guaranteed protection clauses as soon as they joined digital platforms – covering accidents, for example, or compensation when algorithms fail, among other things. That would be an important step towards bringing other issues to the negotiating table, such as the share each party receives for every task successfully completed on the platform. This does not happen today. Young people on platforms are left to fend for themselves, with no one to protect them.
Why should young workers join a union?
Young people should join a union because that is where they will find a source of hope and collective struggle for fairer social and working conditions. This is especially true once they realize that their future depends on employment and that, together, they can push for better working conditions, for training and professional qualifications and for more effective use of today’s tools for mobilizing young people.
How can unions better attract young members? Unions can attract more young people by organizing recreational activities and campaigns that respond to their real challenges and interests. This includes campaigns at universities on the role of young people in the labour market and in building fairer jobs and working conditions for youth. That way, they will understand that they are not coming to the union to seek benefits but to build the future they deserve, and that they themselves play an important role in that process.
What is your message to governments this World Day for Decent Work? My message to governments on this important day is that young people are not an equation to be managed. They are the driving force behind the development of countries and peoples and behind a more harmonious and predictable future, because young people will always be the lifeblood of every nation that dreams of prospering. Young people should not be treated as a bet on the future but as an investment in the present.
Find out more about the World Day for Decent Work from the International Trade Union Confederation.

articles.title_orig: Jaguar Unveils £130,000 Electric Car in British Brand’s Reboot
articles.title_zh: Jaguar Unveils £130,000 Electric Car in British Brand’s Reboot
articles.content_orig:
Jaguar has revealed its new electric car two years after its controversial rebranding sparked a backlash with the firm accused of going "woke".
The unveiling of the all-electric Type 01 is a gamble for parent company JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy.
The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.
But it comes at a hefty price tag with a minimum cost of £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US.
The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.
The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".
However, the unveiling of the Type 01 on Tuesday was met with mixed reactions on social media.
"Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its divisive design.
Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that the new design was an "unmitigated catastrophe" that looked like a hearse and lacked any "memorable Jaguar flourish".
But car journalist Steve Fowler said the Type 01 looked "incredible" and made him "proud to be British".
"Not everyone will like it - that's fine. Not everyone has to!" he wrote on X.
Alistair Weaver from vehicle sales platform Edmunds said Jaguar deserved some credit for the Type 01's looks, despite it being "polarising".
"If Jaguar designed a car that looked like anything else, it would have had no hope," Weaver told the BBC.
But the firm faces an uphill battle in the US, where EVs are becoming less popular , he added.
This launch was always bound to attract attention, after the company caused waves with the initial unveiling of its new direction.
In 2024 Jaguar released a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in the ad at all.
Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to show off a pair of radical concept cars , in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes.
Concept cars are mock-ups built to demonstrate an idea, rather than to work when on the road.
Acknowledging that they might prove controversial he quipped: "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody".
The event, heralding Jaguar's future as a luxury all-electric marque , triggered a furious backlash in the press and on social media.
Critics claimed JLR was betraying its heritage in favour of going "woke". Even the colour chosen for the launch was derided as "Barbie pink", as culture wars erupted around it.
The reception appeared to catch JLR by surprise. The reinvention of Jaguar as a luxury electric brand was part of a wide-ranging strategy set out by the company in early 2023, in which it pledged to invest £15bn in new models and technologies.
At the time, Jaguar itself was struggling. The badge, which was once an intrinsic part of Swinging Sixties British cool, had lost its lustre. Where in the past it had supplied E-Types to Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen, it now struggled to sell upmarket saloons and SUVs to middle-ranking corporate executives, who generally preferred Audis and BMWs.
"Jaguar's core demographic, despite the uproar, gave up on the brand years ago, so they effectively had nothing to lose," said Matthias Schmidt of Schmidt Automotive Research.
JLR wound down production of its old Jaguar models in 2024 and 2025. The "woke" row, while it may have made life briefly uncomfortable for the company's leadership, did at least keep the brand in the public consciousness.
The GT is expected to be the first of three new electric designs from Jaguar.
Since then JLR has parted ways with the agency behind the rebranding campaign, and the company also has a new chief executive.
But the future of Jaguar itself still hangs in the balance.
"I think it really is a last throw of the dice," says journalist Steve Fowler. "JLR has struggled to make serious money with Jaguar in the past, and that's what it's all about."

articles.title_orig: Nadia Comăneci Sends a Message to the Judo World in Baku
articles.title_zh: Nadia Comăneci Sends a Message to the Judo World in Baku
articles.content_orig:
As the 2026 Baku World Championships brings together the finest judoka on the planet, Nadia Comăneci wished to address a message to all those taking part. Coming from an athlete whose achievements and influence have inspired generations, her words carry a resonance that reaches far beyond the competition itself.
“As an IJF Ambassador and an athlete, I know that great performances are built through discipline, courage and determination. To all the athletes here competing in Baku, compete with pride, respect your opponent and give your best on the tatami. Medals are remembered but so is character and the inspiration we leave to the next generation. Wishing you all an unforgettable world championship.”
Her message reflects the very essence of judo: the search for excellence, certainly, but also the respect, humility and responsibility that give sporting achievement its deepest meaning.

articles.title_orig: Quiles will become Moto3 World Champion if...
articles.title_zh: Quiles will become Moto3 World Champion if...
articles.content_orig:
Quiles heads to Indonesia for his next chance at match point, but what does the #28 need to do to clinch the title?
It’s a big weekend for Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team), who has another opportunity to be crowned Champion this weekend. Quiles enters the weekend with a 127-point advantage over his rivals, and with just 125 points remaining up for grabs after Indonesia, the #28 is now faced with another opportunity to be crowned Moto3 World Champion.
Simply put, if Quiles leaves Indonesia with at least a 125-point advantage, then he will be crowned 2026 Moto3 World Champion. Four riders remain in mathematical contention, with Quiles, Alvaro Carpe (Red Bull KTM Ajo), David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) and Brian Uriarte (Red Bull KTM Ajo) all facing a pivotal weekend.
Ultimately, Quiles has the opportunity to control his own destiny. A victory would crown him World Champion regardless of other results, whilst P2 would also be enough if Almansa finishes P3 or lower. Meanwhile, a third-place finish will secure Quiles the title if Almansa were to finish P4 or below on Sunday.
Finishing outside the podium positions brings Carpe into contention. If Quiles finishes fourth, Carpe would need to score P2 or worse, while Almansa would need to finish P5 or lower. Anything outside of the top five (P6 or lower) for Quiles brings Uriarte back into the picture, increasing the complications.
It has already been an incredible season for Quiles, who has earned nine race wins and 14 podiums from the opening 16 rounds. The #28 has already scored 52 points more than his entire 2025 campaign, underlining just how impressive his form has been this year.

articles.title_orig: Collins and Jackson Clash in First Debate of Crucial Maine Senate Race
articles.title_zh: Collins and Jackson Clash in First Debate of Crucial Maine Senate Race
articles.content_orig:
Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.
Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.
Collins’ defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.
Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.
Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democrat presidential candidates in every election since 1992.
Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.
Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.
“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.
“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”
Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

articles.title_orig: Pacific nations insist world must increase efforts to meet global warming limit
articles.title_zh: Pacific nations insist world must increase efforts to meet global warming limit
articles.content_orig:
NADI, Fiji, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Global governments must increase efforts to reduce emissions because the planet is "hurtling past" a critical temperature target that would restrain sea level rises and extreme weather, delegates at a major climate conference in Fiji said on Wednesday.
Pacific nations, which are among the world's most vulnerable to climate change, are trying to lock their priorities into global climate negotiations at the ministerial meeting in Fiji, a precursor to the COP31 forum in Turkey in November.
Among those priorities are securing better access to climate finance, protecting oceans, and making sure the target of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels is honoured, despite projections from the UN that it will soon be exceeded.
"We are hurtling past the 1.5-degree temperature limit," Fijian climate minister Lynda Tabuya told representatives from more than 50 countries at the start of pre-COP ministerial negotiations.
The data simply confirm what Pacific nations can see, she said: "The tide that reaches our homes, the pale reef our grandmothers no longer recognise, the villages we have already had to relocate."
"Overshoot (of the target) is not a verdict we accept quietly ... keeping 1.5 alive is the primary legal obligation and duty we are here to uphold."
On Tuesday, representatives from around 30 nations gathered in Fiji after a visit to the vulnerable atoll nation of Tuvalu and adopted a declaration calling for "deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions."
The delegation, which includes Pacific island leaders and representatives from countries including France, India and the United Arab Emirates, saw heavy machinery digging sand and creating new land that can withstand rising seas.
"Every fraction of a degree of warming accelerates the impacts of climate change and increases the risk of irreversible loss and damage," said the declaration, whose title, Taku Pakasoa, is the Tuvaluan concept of the strength found in unity and collective action.
Exceeding a 1.5-degree rise — and significant environmental damage — was now unavoidable, said Dechen Tsering, director of the Regional Office of Asia Pacific at the UN Environment Programme.
"Pacific risks will outlast the temperature peak," she said. "Each additional 100 years above 1.5 degrees would commit the world to around 40 centimetres (15.8 inches) of additional median sea level rise by 2300 compared with the pathway without overshoot."
Turkey is hosting COP31 in the coastal city of Antalya and Australia is leading the negotiations.
The pre-COP events in Fiji and Tuvalu this week will shape what is possible at COP31, said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen.
"This region is home to some of the world's strongest climate voices," he said, adding that Pacific advocacy was vital in the adoption of the 1.5 degree goal at COP21 in Paris in 2015. "It's also experiencing the most direct impacts."
Turkey's environment minister Murat Kurum, who is president of COP31, said limiting overshoot of the target was the summit's clear common goal.
"I believe in this wholeheartedly," he said.
(Reporting by Peter Hobson in Nadi and Renju Jose in Sydney; Editing by Sonali Paul and Kim Coghill)

articles.title_orig: Why athletes from around the world are heading to a remote town in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Why athletes from around the world are heading to a remote town in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Portuguese entrepreneur Pedro Queirós could spend his vacation relaxing on a beach with his family, but instead, every year since 2021, he has chosen to spend at least a month at a training camp in a small Kenyan town, running for a few hours a day around 8,000 feet above sea level.
“I’m an amateur runner, I don’t have sponsors, I’m not paid,” the 45-year-old told CNN. “But I love the sport, and Kenya is the only place that gives me the opportunity to become the athlete I’ve always dreamed of being.”
Queirós’s running romance is one that many will recognize. He ran his first 5K (3.1-mile race) a decade ago and fell in love. He pushed the distance, started reading about the sport’s history, researched nutrition and bought a GPS smartwatch.
By the end of the Covid pandemic, as he prepared for the London Marathon, he became curious about a Kenyan town he’d read about: Iten. Kenyan runners have collectively won 38 Olympic gold medals, mostly in long-distance events. Some of the best have trained in Iten.
“I started becoming curious,” Queirós said. “What are they doing differently in Africa? And what does it take to be a champion?”
It took just one stay at the training camp to answer the question. He said that after six weeks at Iten’s High-Altitude Training Center his performance improved dramatically, with his marathon time dropping to a very respectable 2 hours and 38 minutes. It’s the reason why he’s been back eight times since, always before a physical challenge, whether a long-distance race or climbing some of the world’s highest peaks. It’s the kind of performance-boosting impact that has earned Iten its nickname, the “home of champions.”
Today, the High-Altitude Training Center is a small campus with accommodation, a gym, a swimming pool, a sauna, a private tarmac track and nature on every side. It welcomes up to 90 people in high season, half of them international visitors. It’s one of roughly a dozen training centers in Iten now — but when it launched, it was pioneering.
“When I thought about opening the training center in 1997, there was nothing in Iten,” long-distance runner and three-time Olympian Lornah Kiplagat said of the former agricultural outpost 200 miles northwest of Nairobi. “No hotel, no roads, and certainly no tourists.”
At the time, the Rift Valley-native was 23 and had just started to compete abroad, winning the Los Angeles Marathon, the 25 Berlin, Zurich’s Greifenseelauf, USA’s Boilermaker Road Race and the Netherlands’ Tilburg Ten Miles all that same year. She was training everywhere from Albuquerque, New Mexico, to Davos, Switzerland. “I realized that there was objectively no better place to train than home,” she said.
Iten’s altitude is well above the roughly 6,000 feet of some of the world’s most famous high-altitude training bases, forcing the body to adapt to lower oxygen levels and dramatically improving endurance and stamina. The climate averages around 18 degrees Celsius (64.4 degrees Fahrenheit) year-round, and the terrain is challenging but beautiful.
In 1999, Kiplagat opened the training center, inviting some local peers to train with her on Iten’s famous red clay roads. She also opened the center to Kenyan girls, to encourage them to take up running, even casually, in a safe space.
“As a group, we were winning big competitions, and Western media started to wonder where we were training,” she said. “Of course, we mentioned the High-Altitude Training Center. Most had never heard of it before. That’s how, step by step, we became known worldwide for producing some of the best distance runners in the world.”
The Hollywood hits filmed in Africa
Since 2004, the center has opened to international athletes, including British three-time London Marathon winner Paula Radcliffe and Olympic gold medalists Mo Farah and Sifan Hassan. But it took a global pandemic to truly make the center a global destination.
Covid-19 lockdowns led to a surge in popularity for running. Afterward, “Runcations” and “race-cations” took off, with runners increasingly traveling abroad specifically to run. Hotels and businesses adapted. So did Kiplagat.
“Running became so popular, we were receiving so many requests from recreational runners too. So, we decided to open our doors to welcome them as well,” she said.
As did the rest of the town. Compared to when she opened the center, Iten is now unrecognizable, Kiplagat said. Queirós has witnessed the changes over the past five years: “The only thing that hasn’t changed is the altitude. The town is bigger, more crowded, and the people coming to train are far more diverse.”
Today, staying at the HATC and having access to its gym, track and sauna costs around 50 euros ($57) per day. While some choose to follow their own program, or to join groups of other athletes training there for free, people like Queirós prefer to pay for the center’s coaches and pacers for around 5 euros ($6) per session. The center has five full-time coaches, and a wide network of pacers around the town.
According to figures compiled by former academic and now-environment officer Joyce Kenei, annual sports tourists in Iten rose from around 300 in 2010 to more than 3,000 by 2025 . An entire sports-tourism economy has grown around them: training camps, accommodation, businesses and support services.
Sports brands have discovered Iten’s potential too. Decathlon’s running label Kiprun has opened 42 House , a residential training facility supporting elite runners. Half of the training centers founded in Iten since the HATC opened were started by foreigners, Kenei told CNN.
But Kiplagat stays grounded in her model — one of the only ones, she says, that gives back to the town. The center has trained nearly 300 local students for free, many of whom went on to win full scholarships to Ivy League schools in the US.
“We really built a system that’s equally welcoming to both locals and internationals, and really pushes everyone to be at their best,” she said.
“Western media show the chaotic part of the country,” she added. “But I take great pride in Kenya, and I love the role the High Altitude Training Center plays in showing it to travelers.”

articles.title_orig: World faces risk cocktail from AI, oil and debt, says IMF chief
articles.title_zh: World faces risk cocktail from AI, oil and debt, says IMF chief
articles.content_orig:
Global governments must act urgently to address challenges from an unbalanced AI boom , a prolonged energy shock and record debt piles, the International Monetary Fund said as it prepares to host economy chiefs from around the world next week.
The rush to develop artificial intelligence is delivering a growth spurt that’s so far confined to a handful of countries, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the annual IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok next week.
Meantime the squeeze on key commodity supplies due to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine is set to continue into 2027, and soaring bond yields have left governments that amassed too much debt under mounting budget pressure, Georgieva said — calling advanced economies the “worst offenders” on the latter count.
“The AI building boom is inflationary. The energy and food shocks are inflationary. Tariffs, defense spending, and high public debt can be inflationary,” Georgieva said. She called for a “prudently hawkish bias” on the part of central banks, and said countries that have gotten used to running large budget deficits are in for “some very tough political choices.”
ALSO READ: IMF: Targeted aid best shields poor from price shocks
The weeklong Bangkok gathering of top finance ministers and central bank governors takes place against a backdrop of turbulence in sovereign debt markets, as yields on US, European and Japanese bonds hit multi-decade highs. Total global debt has now surpassed $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance.
“Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates,” Georgieva said. “Higher interest rates now put an end to that.”
By contrast, the wave of AI investment — and expectations for the economic gains it will deliver — keeps propeling stocks to new highs, and has delivered record exports for Asia’s powerhouse producers of chips and other equipment.
The bond selloff got underway after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, choking off fuel supplies and raising costs worldwide. Georgieva said the energy shock has been “large but contained” so far. But she warned that “price pressures may build further as demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season and as countries replenish reserves.”
READ MORE: IMF chief says world economy faces multiple risks despite resilience
The AI buildout is adding to energy demand, and it also risks widening economic inequalities, Georgieva said. “Growth in AI-related trade reflects the investment boom in economies embedded in its value chain,” she said, but “it largely bypasses most others.”

articles.title_orig: Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
articles.title_zh: Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
articles.content_orig:
Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023.
"We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi.
By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.
The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies."
As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places.
Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer.
The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire.
Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours.
"On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me.
"From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed."
An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz.
Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby.
Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later.
As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe.
The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place.  "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here."
The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen.
The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here.
On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping.
Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards.
Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis.
"This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry."
"Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone."
While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed.
Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated.
Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here.
They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. Dalit and Achi are determined to return too.
"We'll come back for the memory of Shiri and for the people that didn't have the chance to live here, and for the memory of my parents, and to continue our roots, and for my children, because this is our home," Dalit says.
However, she, Achi and their children - currently displaced and living in an apartment in a town further north - face a two-year wait for Nir Oz to reopen fully.
"Terrorists penetrated 97% of the households and burned down almost 50%," says Emi Palmor, director of the rebuilding project. "Now it's the only place in Israel that has to be completely demolished and completely replanned."
She says that it is a difficult balance to redesign the kibbutz so that it feels like home but does not cause new trauma to those who return.
"It's a huge debate – a very painful debate," Emi says. "Some people say, 'If I come back here, I want the entire area to look serene. I don't have to be reminded because I remember every day the people I lost.' Other people say, 'There is such denial – if we will take down the last houses, who will ever believe?'"
About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage after an estimated 6,000 Palestinians streamed across the Gaza border during the attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN.
Despite the US-brokered ceasefire deal which brought the last hostages home a year ago, violence has continued, including near-daily Israeli attacks on Gaza. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced and much of the territory is in ruins. US President Donald Trump's peace plan is at an impasse.
For Israelis, there are outstanding questions over accountability for the failure of Israel's security forces to have prevented the 7 October attacks. People from Nir Oz favour a comprehensive state commission of inquiry and still have major security concerns.
Survivors, including the Aharons, suffer from post-traumatic stress. Dalit recalls how her eldest son, Uri, turned nine on 7 October 2023 - when they spent the day hiding in their bomb shelter. "He told me, 'Mum, I don't want to die on my birthday,'" she says. "You know people don't understand that we still live this horrible day."

articles.title_orig: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy
articles.title_zh: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy
articles.content_orig:
There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitive
B ear with me, because there is some backstory to get through before we can talk about the book I am actually here to review. Back in 1984, Stephen King and Peter Straub collaborated on the fantasy novel The Talisman. Like all the best King stories, it follows a young boy: in this case Jack Sawyer, 12, whose mother, Lily, is dying. Jack learns that a magical object called the Talisman might save her – if he can find it in a parallel world known as the Territories. Straub and King followed this up in 2001 with Black House , in which an adult Jack investigates a series of child murders that turn out to have disturbing links to the Territories.
The books are very different: one a coming-of-age cross-country quest, in which Jack flips back and forth between two versions of the US; the other a fantastical and horror-inflected murder mystery. Both are brilliant and enduring classics which will always have a place on my bookshelves – I reread both of them, all 1,800-odd pages, to prepare for Other Worlds Than These and was as swept away and delighted as the first time round.
So: in 2013 Straub had an idea for a final volume in the Talisman trilogy, drawing as Black House does from a real-life series of murders, and returning Jack (previously left on a bit of a cliffhanger) to the fray. King didn’t pick up on it back then, and Straub died in 2022 . Now King is 79, and, as he writes in a somewhat valedictory afterword, “it’s time to think about tidying up, as much as such things are possible for a writer whose mind is still crammed with cool ideas”. So he went back to that old idea – the original email lost, but the concept of a “series of motiveless, brutal crimes” in the Far West of the Territories, as Straub put it, at the story’s heart.
Jack, “his tide … going out”, is now 57. An aimless, lonely émigré to the Territories, he is sent on a mission by the two-bit despot he now depressingly reports to. He’s to travel through the toxic Blasted Lands to gather information on the Great Gorge, a mysterious area of “growing danger” that Governor Youngblood wants to know more about. Flipping back and forth between “America-side” and the Territories, Jack learns that an old policeman friend has gone missing on the trail of a pair of “murderin’ kids” who have been leaving a swathe of bodies in their wake in Nebraska. These kids are, he’s told, “infested” by demons – and the infestation is spreading to the children of the Territories.
For the true King fan (the “Constant Reader”, as he puts it), there are moments of shivering joy in Other Worlds Than These – not least in the title, which draws from a key scene in King’s The Gunslinger. I could never not find pleasure in a billy-bumbler (a dog-like creature), or in memories of Wolf, a wonderful creation from The Talisman, or in references to chief gunslinger Roland Deschain from the Dark Tower series. As befits King, there are moments of true horror too, and good ones, as the teenage infection spreads across the Territories.
But I cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tome. For one, it would be pointless to read it without previously having read The Talisman and Black House (and if I’m honest, probably the seven-volume Dark Tower sequence too). And even for the Constant Reader, this is really not vintage King. I would have said that I’d follow Jack Sawyer anywhere, but as Ole Travellin’ Jack crisscrossed his way across the dry desert land of the Territories, his journey started to feel endless, and endlessly repetitive. As Jack’s crew are gearing up to cross yet another rickety bridge over yet another gaping chasm, one character even makes this point when they spot it. “Oh God … talk about repetition.” I hear you, fella! Jack himself does it: “Another echo. They’re becoming tiresome,” he says, in a rather too on-the-nose comment about the eerie (not so eerie the nth time they’re mentioned) similarities between the US and the Territories.
Is this deliberate? Yes, undoubtedly: “ka [destiny] is a wheel”, as we’ve been told (more than once); Jack, as Roland did before him, is treading the path laid out for him in an endless cycle. But this time round, it all gets a little portentous, self-referential and self-indulgent – and, dare I say it, boring.
I still think Stephen King is a genius. I still think The Talisman is the perfect coming-of-age dark fantasy novel. So thank you for the endless hours of reading pleasure, Mr King. But unlike its predecessors, Other Worlds Than These will not be going on my reread shelf.
after newsletter promotion

articles.title_orig: World Shipping Council launch digital global Whale Chart with HUB Ocean
articles.title_zh: World Shipping Council launch digital global Whale Chart with HUB Ocean
articles.content_orig:
Kimberly Mathisen (CEO, HUB Ocean) & Joe Kramek (President & CEO, World Shipping Council) - download a high-resolution version of this image.
7 October 2026 – The World Shipping Council (WSC), in partnership with HUB Ocean, today launched a digital version of the WSC Whale Chart, making global information on measures to protect whales from ships even more accessible.
Since its initial launch in 2023, WSC’s Whale Chart was the first global mapping of all known mandatory and voluntary governmental measures designed to reduce harm to whales from vessels. These include speed restrictions, routing measures, areas to be avoided and measures addressing underwater radiated noise.
By partnering with HUB Ocean to produce the digital Whale Chart, these measures are now easier to explore, easier to keep up to date, and can plug directly into digital tools and operational systems.
“Mariners operate across many different jurisdictions, and the measures in place to protect whales vary from country to country and region to region. Bringing this information together digitally and making it available to mariners on the bridges of the ships they are navigating makes it easier to use in voyage planning and helps crews see where changing course or slowing down can make a real difference,” said Joe Kramek, President & CEO of the World Shipping Council.
“The Whale Chart has already become an important reference point for the shipping industry,” said Kimberly Mathisen, CEO of HUB Ocean. “Our hope is that by making this information easier to work with, it becomes part of more decisions, more voyages and ultimately more action to protect whales.”
The Whale Chart and all its underlying datasets are now available through HUB Ocean’s Ocean Data Platform, an open, cloud-based geospatial platform that turns ocean data into insight and action.
Bringing the Whale Chart into that ecosystem means it can be explored alongside other authoritative datasets such as marine protected areas and other ocean intelligence layers, supporting richer insights and decisions for mariners, ship operators, governments and researchers alike.
Alongside the new digital platform, WSC has released the fourth edition of the WSC Whale Chart handbook, providing a quick regional overview of whale protection measures. The digital Whale Chart complements this with more detailed, searchable and most current information for specific voyage areas.
Whales travel across national boundaries and through some of the world’s busiest shipping routes. Where shipping traffic and whale activity overlap, separating ships from whales is the most effective way to reduce the risk of collisions. Where separation is not possible, measures such as speed reductions can help reduce the risk and severity of ship strikes while also limiting underwater noise.
WSC will continue to update the WSC Whale Chart as measures change and new information becomes available.
The digital WSC Whale Chart on the Ocean Data Platform is available here and a preview is available on WSC’s Whales webpage .
About World Shipping Council
The World Shipping Council is the united voice of liner shipping, working with policymakers and industry groups to shape the future growth of a socially responsible, environmentally sustainable, safe, and secure shipping industry. We are a non-profit trade association with offices in Brussels, London, Singapore and Washington, D.C.
80% of everything we buy has come by ship. World Shipping Council members are the international container and vehicle carriers that make global trade possible by offering cost efficient and effective transport for everything from raw materials, food and machinery parts to consumer essentials like medication, clothes and electronics.
Read more at www.worldshipping.org
HUB Ocean is an independent non-profit foundation, dedicated to unlocking the power of data to protect and restore ocean health. The organization has built the performant geospatial and cloud-based Ocean Data Platform, giving scientists, experts, and organizations seamless access to fit-for-purpose ocean data from both public and private sources. Built for interoperability and speed, the platform is designed to connect a federated ocean data ecosystem and accelerate collective action for a sustainable ocean.

articles.title_orig: Linux Foundation Launches OpenGrid to Build Open, Shared Infrastructure for the World's Electric Grid
articles.title_zh: Linux Foundation Launches OpenGrid to Build Open, Shared Infrastructure for the World's Electric Grid
articles.content_orig:
New open source initiative integrates and builds a data platform and tools to accelerate grid planning and energy infrastructure deployments worldwide
PRAGUE , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Open Source Summit Europe – The Linux Foundation , the nonprofit organization enabling mass innovation through open source, today announced the launch of OpenGrid, a new initiative building open source infrastructure to modernize power grid planning worldwide. Hosted by the Linux Foundation, OpenGrid creates a neutral, interoperable foundation that allows planners to work across the commercial and open source software they already use, helping reduce the time, cost and technical barriers involved in planning the infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing electricity demand.
Grid planning has become a critical bottleneck as electricity demand grows, new data center and industrial loads come online and more generation and storage seek connection. More than 2,500 gigawatts of generation, storage and large-load projects are currently pending in grid connection queues worldwide, while annual grid investment needs to roughly double to more than $600 billion by 2030 . Meeting long-term energy needs will require adding or replacing 80 million kilometers of power lines by 2040, yet planning remains constrained by fragmented data, incompatible software and modeling capabilities that are inaccessible to many institutions and countries.
"Open source has repeatedly shown that shared architecture and interoperability accelerate innovation across entire industries," said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. "OpenGrid will bring the proven model of open collaboration to grid planning for faster and more reliable deployment. The Linux Foundation's neutral governance will ensure durability, longevity and usability of the technologies that support essential public-interest infrastructure."
OpenGrid is not developing a single replacement for existing grid planning software. Instead, it provides a shared data and interoperability layer that allows existing commercial and open source tools to work together. Its foundational efforts will include open standards and schemas, programmatic APIs and a centralized Data Hub for validated, model-ready datasets. Its first lighthouse application, the OpenGrid Translator, is in development for release in 2027 and will enable data and models to move between widely used commercial platforms and open source tools.
Access to modern planning capabilities is particularly uneven in fast-growing markets. At the same time, emerging economies are expected to account for nearly 80% of global electricity demand growth through 2030 . OpenGrid aims to give planning teams everywhere access to high-quality modeling capabilities, while enabling regulators, advocates and other stakeholders to inspect the models and data informing major infrastructure decisions.
"Reliable electricity supports healthier lives, stronger communities and economic opportunity, but delivering it requires credible plans. Today, too many plans rely on data others cannot verify and tools much of the world cannot afford," said Alice Yake, vice president of BE-GRIDS and chair of the OpenGrid Management Committee. "OpenGrid changes that: open data, open standards and access to planning tools that any utility, regulator or country can inspect and use."
Over time, the OpenGrid ecosystem plans to expand to include open solvers, no-code graphical interfaces, standardized planning workflows and integrations that use AI to support data preparation. By providing transparent, repeatable and accessible planning infrastructure, OpenGrid aims to help planners, infrastructure owners, regulators and communities work from a common technical foundation and make infrastructure decisions with greater confidence faster.
OpenGrid launches with support from Breakthrough Energy GRIDS, Global Grid Catalyst, Connected Grid Initiative and Google.org, with technical delivery partners including Open Energy Transition, Tapestry, TransitionZero and QXT Energy.
Organizations, researchers, regulators and community members interested in contributing to OpenGrid or learning more are encouraged to visit https://www.opengrid.org .
"Electricity systems are going through some pretty radical changes, with many new variable producers, storage and consumers connecting to the grid. OpenGrid supports the infrastructure we need to get quick consensus on how the energy transition should proceed, and to foster the innovation we need to drive it forward faster."
– Tom Brown, Professor of Digital Transformation in Energy Systems, TU Berlin and Managing Director, PyPSA Labs
"Planners shouldn't have to choose between the tools they already use and the open ones now emerging. Building enterprise-grade, open modeling software with Scenario Builder showed us how much time is lost moving data and models between formats. OpenGrid's shared standards and translators tackle that directly, and we're glad to help build them, so that planners anywhere can pick up a model, inspect it, use it and make decisions that cut the time it takes to build clean energy at scale."
– Matt Gray, Co-Founder and CEO, TransitionZero
"Accelerating scientific progress requires turning foundational research and open data into real-world solutions. Power grids are among humanity's most complex engineering systems, yet modeling them is too often limited by fragmented tools and closed data. OpenGrid will provide the shared digital foundation needed to make faster, more evidence-based decisions and ultimately strengthen our global grid infrastructure."
– Joseph Hassine, Scaled Impact Lead, Google.org
"OpenGrid is the catalyst that the power and energy industry needs to drive new software innovations that ultimately will produce better and faster decision making for the power grid. We keep hearing that these times are unprecedented and yet we have seen very few changes in the power software space. OpenGrid's ambitions to demonstrate that open source can be the driver for much needed innovation is something that QXT Energy is enthusiastic to support."
– José Daniel Lara, Co-Founder and CTO, QXT Energy
"The accelerating complexity of the modern power system demands better integration of economic and reliability planning tools, as well as coordinated planning across the transmission and distribution networks. OpenGrid is tackling this ambitious challenge by enabling these diverse tools, whether open source or commercial, to work together and by providing validated datasets. This has the potential to revolutionize grid planning across the globe."
– Debbie Lew, Executive Director, Energy Systems Integration Group (ESIG)
"At OpenET, we make water use data open and accessible, so I've seen firsthand how a shared baseline builds trust among diverse stakeholders. That experience convinces me that open data infrastructure is essential to sound resource management. By giving planners, regulators and communities a common ground truth they can all inspect and understand, OpenGrid will help them make the decisions the energy transition demands."
– Luis Villa, Board Chair, OpenET, Inc.
"Transparent and neutral governance ensures that all interested users have access to the tools in this initiative. It allows users to decide what is best for their purposes, and it keeps the door open for new tool development to foster innovation and avoid lock-in. Transparency in decision-making creates community buy-in. When parties come together on shared infrastructure, working toward common objectives and the methods and results can be vetted by many parties, this builds the trust and sense of fairness and legitimacy that will be necessary for OpenGrid to be successful."
– Karin Wadsack, Executive Director, Global Power System Transformation Consortium
About the Linux Foundation The Linux Foundation is the world's leading home for collaboration on open source software, hardware, standards, and data

articles.title_orig: Satellite images show attack jets, vehicles at new China-Laos base
articles.title_zh: Satellite images show attack jets, vehicles at new China-Laos base
articles.content_orig:
Tuesday, October 6, 2026 75° Today's Paper
By Greg Torode and Poppy McPherson / Reuters
Today • Last updated
                                            2:13 p.m.
VANTOR/HANDOUT VIA REUTERS
A satellite image shows what security analysts believe are Y-8 light attack fighters and support vehicles at a new China-Laos joint training facility in Ban Keun, Vientiane Province, Laos, on Sept. 30.
VANTOR/HANDOUT VIA REUTERS
A satellite image shows a new China-Laos joint training facility, with a runway that is being expanded, in Ban Keun, Vientiane Province, Laos, on Sept. 30.
HONG KONG/BANGKOK >> Light attack aircraft and military vehicles have arrived at the new China-Laos joint training facility announced on Sept. 29, according to satellite images reviewed by Reuters.
The images, taken by commercial satellite provider Vantor, show what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still being built — China’s latest expansion of its overseas military presence.
Taken on September 30, the day after China’s defense ministry announced it had set up the facility at Ban Keun outside the capital Vientiane, the images also show extensive construction work around the runway.
The swift development of the new facility is being closely watched by regional military attaches and security scholars, some of whom say its construction potentially marks China’s first fully fledged overseas military base in Southeast Asia.
Despite more than 20 years of intense military modernisation, China is widely perceived to lack a strong network of overseas facilities beyond the South China Sea, port access in Ream, Cambodia and a logistics base in Djibouti.
Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said the selection of Ban Keun for a facility that the People’s Liberation Army could access “is likely more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need.”
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
“Laos does have some geostrategic value as an accessible foothold in mainland Southeast Asia, given its shared border with China and infrastructure links, including (its) railway,” Vandenbrink said.
The Chinese defense ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
The Lao embassy in Bangkok and the Lao foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Singapore-based security analysts Collin Koh and Alexander Neill, as well as Vantor specialists, said the planes appeared to be Hongdu JL-8 aircraft, which both the Chinese and Lao air forces operate.
Also known as the K-8, the two-seater aircraft is extensively used for training as well as having light attack capabilities. It was jointly developed by China and Pakistan and is exported to other militaries.
Laos currently has four of the planes, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies’ annual assessment of the world’s militaries. Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, described the Laotian planes as being of “questionable serviceability”.
As construction continues, diplomats and analysts are keeping watch for any sign of air defenses, ammunition and fuel storage as well as surveillance facilities — all of which could point to the base serving broader military functions beyond training.
Neill said while the airfield looked relatively short and innocuous at present, it could in future serve larger aircraft, including signals intelligence and electronic-surveillance planes to extend China’s reach into Southeast Asia.
“It looks like the airfield has been engineered to accommodate a runway extension allowing larger aircraft to operate,” said Neill, an adjunct fellow at Hawaii’s Pacific Forum think-tank.
In helping Laos build up Ban Keun, China is now occupying a site the US used covertly at the height of the Vietnam War.
During the US war against communist forces in Laos in the 1970s, Ban Keun was an airfield known as “Lima Site 44” used by Air America, an airline discreetly owned by the Central Intelligence Agency, according to records shared with Reuters by Ryan Wolfson-Ford, a Southeast Asia specialist at the Library of Congress.
The airline carried American-backed troops from the country’s Hmong highland minority as well as supplies into rough mountain airstrips known as “Lima Sites”.
As early as 1968, Ban Keun was used as a point from where Air America helicopters delivered Hmong troops to other combat zones, said Dr Joachim Leeker, an academic who has written about the history of the airline.

articles.title_orig: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after surviving a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while "handcuffed and shackled to the bed" in hospital, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two failed lethal injections last Wednesday in Tennessee.
She was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical. Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented.
Pike is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection.
Her lawyers said her prognosis remained unclear, but that "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking.
There had been seven other cases where prisoners survived executions but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
"They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," Denno said. "This has never happened before."
Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, a local journalist who witnessed the attempted execution said that he, too, did not know of "an exact precedent".
Steven Hale, a journalist for the Nashville Banner, said the case raised many questions, including "what must this be like for the victim's family, who for 30 years has been told we are gonna give you justice and justice is us executing Christa Pike".
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong after twice injecting her with the chemical pentobarbital.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he planned to resign.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.
Pike's lawyers are scheduled to appear in court in Nashville on Wednesday. They also plan to hold a news conference outside the court.
In their latest update, they repeated their call for Lee to use his powers to commute Pike's sentence to the lower punishment of life in prison without parole.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said on Tuesday that the likelihood of recovering from lethal injection was low.
"Most people who get lethal injection die from it," he told the BBC. "In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa. So, the fact that she survived it... was unusual."
But there remains a lot of uncertainty and many unknowns, he said, including how much of the pentobarbital got into her system, what her blood levels were after the injection and what her recovery will look like.
"I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he noted.
Zivot had previously said the two doses of pentobarbital she received last week would have been enough that, had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation, "she would have surely died".
Instead, Zivot said a possible explanation is that instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
They said on Tuesday that she has endured "severe damage" to her arms.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks information about such cases.
For lethal injections, such incidents have typically occurred due to difficulty obtaining reliable IV access to the veins, though the underlying reason differs from person to person.
In cases the centre has documented, all failures happened before the lethal  drugs could be administered. The last failed lethal injection that was tracked happened earlier this year - also in Tennessee.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.

articles.title_orig: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
articles.title_zh: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
articles.content_orig:
This image provided by U.S. Department of Justice, and contained in a court filing, shows gold bars and cash that was seized from a David J. Rush's home, during a search on May 19, 2026, in Ashburn, Va. U.S. Dept. of Justice via AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty Tuesday in Virginia to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars worth over $40 million, according to court records.
David J. Rush fabricated a "highly classified" government program to justify the acquisition of luxury property in south Florida that he intended to resell for personal profit, according to a court filing. Rush separately concocted a bogus "sensitive government activity" to obtain the gold bars, the filing says.
Rush's fraudulent conduct cost the federal government approximately $194 million in total losses, according to the Justice Department. The losses included over $1.8 million in privately chartered flights that Rush authorized for personal use at the government's expense.
Under questioning from investigators, Rush admitted that he provided a foreign government official with information about the identity of a secret source for the U.S. government, a new court filing says. The filing doesn't specify which country the foreign official represented.
Prosecutors also accuse Rush of lying to colleagues and government contractors about his military and academic credentials and the fake program that he invented, falsely claiming it was authorized by high-ranking U.S. officials.
"Rush used his legitimate government authority and manufactured personal bona fides to create confidence in his directions," the court filing says.
Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, court records show. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff is scheduled to sentence Rush on Jan. 28 in Alexandria, Virginia.
Several months ago, Rush tried to fraudulently authorize the release of $100 million from a government contract, according to Tuesday's filing. He directed somebody else to transfer approximately $145 million to a holding company formed at his direction, then used those funds to acquire four "luxury" properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, the filing says.
In previous court filings, prosecutors said Rush stashed roughly $46 million worth of gold bars from the federal government at his Virginia home. They also accused him of fraudulently claiming tens of thousands of dollars in compensation for military leave after he was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy in 2015.
"Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency immediately referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation turned up evidence of Rush's crimes.
"David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions," Ratcliffe said in a statement.
Rush was arrested after investigators searched his home and seized approximately 300 gold bars, roughly $2 million in U.S. currency and about 35 luxury watches, according to an FBI agent's affidavit. A judge ordered Rush to be held without bond after his initial court appearance earlier this year.
During a hearing in June, defense attorney Jessica Carmichael said Rush wasn't charged initially with any crimes related to the discovery of the gold bars, which she referred to as "basically a nonissue" and "nothing more than a sensational tidbit." She said her client properly obtained the gold bars and kept them locked in a safe in his basement.
"Mr. Rush never claimed they were his," Carmichael said.
Carmichael declined to comment on Rush's guilty plea after Tuesday's hearing.
Authorities say Rush lied about his education and military background on job applications, falsely claiming to be a former Navy pilot who graduated with a bachelor's degree from Clemson University in South Carolina and a master's degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in New York.
Investigators determined that he didn't serve as a Navy pilot and didn't attend either school. Rush enlisted in the Navy in 1997 and was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy Reserve as a lieutenant in 2015, according to the FBI affidavit.

articles.title_orig: Parents of 21 children charged with abuse in ‘house of horrors’ surrogacy scheme
articles.title_zh: Parents of 21 children charged with abuse in ‘house of horrors’ surrogacy scheme
articles.content_orig:
A California couple at the center of a surrogacy scandal was arrested on Tuesday. A law enforcement source confirmed the arrests to CBS News shortly before officials held a news conference to announce the latest developments.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang are being charged with multiple counts, including conspiracy to commit child abuse and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said.
The couple drew national headlines last year after authorities raided their Arcadia mansion in July 2025 and took 21 kids, mostly surrogate-born , into state custody.
Tuesday morning, detectives from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department arrested the couple at their residence. They were then transferred to the Pasadena courthouse to be arraigned, Sheriff Robert Luna said. They both pleaded not guilty and are each being held on a $20 million bond.
A neighbor said Tuesday that helicopters and police could be seen at the couple's mansion and the entire block is taped off.
"What has been publicly filed in the complaint today is incredibly disturbing. It involves horrific punishment and beatings and child abuse," Hochman said at the news conference.
Officials said the investigation began in May 2025 when Zhang brought a 2-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury.
"She appeared to be untruthful with hospital staff about how the injury was sustained and the hospital staff notified law enforcement authorities," Luna said, adding that when Arcadia police went to the home, "what they discovered raised even more serious concerns."
The district attorney said Tuesday that the children were seated for hours a day in three different rooms called "Learning Centers" under the supervision of various nannies at the couple's home, which he called a "house of horrors." The couple kept a system of 32 motion-activated cameras in the various rooms in the Arcadia mansion, he said. Footage from these cameras went to a television near their desk that the couple used to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Hochman said the nannies were caught on video spanking, slapping or hitting the children. One nanny, Chunmei Li,  allegedly struck the 2-month-old baby in the head, the district attorney said. A $105,000 warrant for her arrest was previously issued, but she remains on the run, he said.
Xuan's attorney, Mitchell Krems, said: "My client is innocent. It is the nanny's wrongdoing who went on the run. He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family."
Melissa Brisman, an attorney for two of the surrogates involved in the case, told CBS News, "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system."
Brisman added that it's important surrogacy remains an option for those who need the help to become parents, but said there must "be adequate protections for those who enter the surrogacy system."
"We need to make sure bad actors don't ruin it for everyone else," she said.
On Tuesday, officials said the Arcadia Police Department requested assistance from the LA County Sheriff's Department in early September. A Los Angeles FBI spokesperson confirmed the FBI served a search warrant at the home, separate from a search conducted by the sheriff's department.
"We will continue to work together to pursue justice for all 21 children involved in this case," Luna said.
Maria Castellanos, a surrogate who carried two children for Zhang and Xuan, said after learning of their arrest, "I'm mad that everyone involved couldn't stop this so the kids wouldn't go through everything they went through. I'm just mad with the whole process, the whole thing. It's not just them."
"I trusted Silvia," she said.
Josh  Boswell contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.title_zh: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.
Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy."
But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already "underwhelming" growth this decade.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," Georgieva said.
Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a "positive demand shock" from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world."
On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.
The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. "Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy," Georgieva said.
But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe," she said.
The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. "The AI building boom is inflationary," she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.
Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.
That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades . Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.
Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had "a relatively easy ride" because interest rates stayed below growth rates. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
The interest-to-growth differential is now "much less favourable" and "set to climb higher," she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now "out of reach in the near term."
The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.
After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries' fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.
Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock."
Citing Amara's Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk."
Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.
