New York, USA, 6 October 2026: Jaguar has unveiled Type 01, the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the brand’s history. A luxury four‑door GT that never arrives unnoticed.
Type 01 inspired a celebration of contemporary culture across New York. This was a one‑of‑a‑kind premiere, from large‑scale digital displays in Times Square, DUMBO and the Lower East Side, to its dynamic arrival for an exclusive gathering at STORIED in West Chelsea, zip code 10001.
Type 01 is defined by exuberant proportions, with its low roofline, long bonnet, sleek silhouette and dramatic presence. Starting from a single line and a blank sheet of paper, it is the most aerodynamic and powerful Jaguar road car. A bold, one‑of‑a‑kind that breaks convention, with a clear lineage to the great Jaguars of the past including the E‑type and XJS.
Beneath Type 01’s clean surfaces is a bespoke Jaguar Electric Architecture which offers more than 1,000PS, always with power in reserve, for a drive that is unmistakably Jaguar. Powered by an 850‑volt electrical architecture, it delivers a 400‑mile range (EPA) and adds 200 miles in 13 minutes using 350kW charging. Type 01 represents a new standard of power, aerodynamics and technological advancement for Jaguar.
From its dramatic design to its captivating drive, Type 01 distils the essence of Jaguar into a luxury grand tourer for a new era. Type 01 is the foundation of this British brand, one that makes no compromise between design and engineering in our quest to create objects of desire, just as it was in the days of the E‑type and XJS.
At the world premiere of Type 01 at STORIED in New York, Jaguar announced acclaimed actor Florence Pugh as the inaugural brand ambassador for its new era. Embodying the originality, fearlessness and creative spirit that define Jaguar.
Pugh joined guests and friends of the brand to celebrate the global arrival of Type 01 with a night dedicated to bold creativity and artistic expression. British singer‑songwriter Sienna Spiro, Best New Artist at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, performed an intimate set. Celebrated chef Roze Traoré conceived an exclusive culinary programme inspired by Jaguar's fearless creative vision.
New York provided the brand with an international stage from which to celebrate originality and British innovation – a city where art, fashion, film, music and design create one of the world’s most influential centres of reinvention.
At STORIED NYC, guests encountered a series of product artefacts exploring the artistry that brought the Type 01 vision to life:
The STORIED reveal sequence began with Type 01’s dynamic arrival, driven by António Félix da Costa from the World Championship‑winning Jaguar TCS Racing team.
This was the biggest moment since the Jaguar name was born in 1935. A fitting tribute and a powerful expression of Jaguar's dramatic new era. A new chapter for the brand begins with Type 01. Jaguar is back. Orders open early 2027 with first client deliveries expected in the second half of the year. Prices start from 130,000 GBP.

A luxury four‑door GT, Type 01 embodies Jaguar's renewed vision of modern luxury, combining dramatic design, craftsmanship and innovation to create an unmistakable presence and emotional connection.

articles.title_orig: Jaguar takes a leap into luxury EV market with new £130,000 model
articles.title_zh: Jaguar takes a leap into luxury EV market with new £130,000 model
articles.content_orig:
Jaguar has revealed its new electric car two years after its controversial rebranding sparked a backlash with the firm accused of going "woke".
The unveiling of the all-electric Type 01 marks a gamble for parent company JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy.
The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.
But it comes at a hefty price tag with a minimum cost of £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US.
The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.
The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".
Under normal circumstances, the launch of a car like this might generate few headlines. But in this case the attention has been much greater, and for good reason.
The unveiling of the Type 01 on Tuesday was met with mixed reactions, with some on social media criticising the new car.
"Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its divisive design.
Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that it is an "unmitigated catastrophe" that looks like a hearse and lacks any "memorable Jaguar flourish".
Car journalist Steve Fowler said the Type 01 "looks incredible" and makes him "proud to be British".
"Not everyone will like it - that's fine. Not everyone has to!" he wrote on X.
Alistair Weaver from vehicle sales platform Edmunds said Jaguar deserved some credit for the Type 01's looks, despite it being "polarising".
"If Jaguar designed a car that looked like anything else, it would have had no hope," Weaver told the BBC.
But the firm faces an uphill battle in the US, where EVs are becoming less popular , he added.
In 2024 Jaguar unveiled its new identity to the public. The first step was a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in sight.
Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to unveil a pair of radical concept cars , resplendent in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes. "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody," he quipped.
The event was meant to herald Jaguar's future as a luxury all-electric marque , but it triggered a furious backlash in the press and on social media.
Critics claimed JLR was betraying its heritage in favour of going "woke". Even the colour chosen for the launch was derided as "Barbie pink", as culture wars erupted around it.
The reception appeared to catch JLR by surprise. The reinvention of Jaguar as a luxury electric brand was part of a wide-ranging strategy set out by the company in early 2023, in which it pledged to invest £15bn in new models and technologies.
At the time, Jaguar itself was struggling. The badge, which was once an intrinsic part of Swinging Sixties British cool, had lost its lustre. Where in the past it had supplied E-Types to Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen, it now struggled to sell upmarket saloons and SUVs to middle-ranking corporate executives, who generally preferred Audis and BMWs.
"Jaguar's core demographic, despite the uproar, gave up on the brand years ago, so they effectively had nothing to lose," explains Matthias Schmidt of Schmidt Automotive Research.
JLR wound down production of its old Jaguar models in 2024 and 2025. The "woke" row, while it possibly made life briefly uncomfortable for the company's leadership, did at least keep the Jaguar name in the public consciousness at a time when it was selling very few cars.
"It brought Jaguar from the back pages to the front pages, given that it was dying in a crowded international market," says Schmidt. "Everyone is now talking about what would have been another boring product."
The GT is expected to be the first of three new electric designs from Jaguar.
Since that event in Miami two years ago, McGovern has left the company, JLR has parted ways with the agency behind the controversial rebranding campaign, and the company also has a new chief executive.
But the future of Jaguar itself still hangs in the balance.
"I think it really is a last throw of the dice," says Fowler. "JLR has struggled to make serious money with Jaguar in the past, and that's what it's all about."
The question now is whether enough buyers can be found willing to pay £130,000 for a relatively distinctive upmarket electric car, in a market where they can also choose models from the likes of Porsche, Mercedes-AMG or even fast-growing Chinese brands such as Denza.
"Forget the controversy, the culture wars and the pink concept car," says Ginny Buckley of the electric car website Electrifying.com.
"What ultimately matters is whether Jaguar has built something extraordinary enough to justify blowing up everything it stood for before."
She believes the car is good enough to silence critics, but admits "the next challenge will be getting people to buy it".
Steve Fowler agrees. "The car is good enough to do it," he says. "Whether the Jaguar brand is good enough remains to be seen."

articles.title_orig: From million-dollar mansions to surveillance missions, the life and travels of an alleged Chinese agent
articles.title_zh: From million-dollar mansions to surveillance missions, the life and travels of an alleged Chinese agent
articles.content_orig:
Three years before California realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang was arrested as an alleged Chinese agent , she showed up in San Francisco celebrating the visit of President Xi Jinping.
Zhang was photographed in 2023 wearing a red cap and marching on the street alongside the leader of a Chinese American organization with deep ties to the Beijing government's foreign influence arm.
Soon after the photo was taken, pro-Chinese Communist Party activists there began assaulting protesters of Xi's authoritarian regime — though there is no evidence Zhang was involved in any attacks.
The Orange County mother, 34, is now facing federal prosecution for allegedly surveilling the Taiwanese president's son in Washington last year at the direction of Chinese government officials.
The FBI said it has obtained her text messages with Chinese intelligence officials, plotting and executing a plan to secretly film Taiwan's first son, Lai Ting-yu, and his family in the Seattle suburb where they live.
Investigators even allege they have footage from a neighbor's security camera catching Zhang in the midst of her surveillance mission.
A CBS News investigation reveals the alleged agent's backstory bears striking similarities with infamous suspected Chinese spy Fang "Christine" Fang, who had an intimate relationship with disgraced congressman Eric Swalwell before fleeing to China in 2015 amid an FBI espionage probe.
Like Fang, Zhang attended the University of International Relations in Beijing, which is run by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's intelligence agency and secret police.
In a criminal complaint filed in a Los Angeles court, FBI counterintelligence special agent Kevin Holt wrote that the ministry "recruits heavily" from the university.
After moving to the U.S., Zhang studied at the University of Southern California and got her real estate license in 2016.
She built her business as a realtor with Irvine-based JC Pacific Corp over the next decade, listing over 130 properties, according to Zillow, with prices ranging from the hundreds of thousands to upwards of $8 million.
Zhang and her husband, a fellow realtor at JC Pacific, bought their six-bedroom, 6,030-square-foot home for $5.65 million in 2024, records show. They sold the property in June for $6 million.
Her Instagram page shows curated photos of Zhang in designer clothing, dining at expensive restaurants, taking trips around the U.S. and Canada, and shopping at luxury stores with a friend in Paris last year.
Similar to Fang, she became involved in advocacy groups and events for Chinese Americans.
In 2022 she attended an "entrepreneurship competition" for Chinese students with Chinese government consulate officials, and was honored at an event for "Chinese young elites in the United States" the same year where she was given a " young entrepreneur " award.
Her involvement in the All American Chinese Association brought her in contact with officials who had deep ties to the Chinese government.
AACA's leader, Cai Chenghua, was vice chair of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, a U.S. group so close to the Beijing government it had to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act as an influence arm of the Chinese Communist Party.
In 2022 Cai helped organize a celebration of China's National Day at which the Los Angeles consul general Zhang Ping urged Chinese Americans to oppose "Taiwan independence" and support China's "complete reunification."
AACA bused in pro-China supporters to San Francisco for President Xi's visit in November 2023. Zhang was photographed alongside Cai, wearing matching red caps behind an AACA banner.
AACA board member Tian Jun is also a committee member in the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office, which became part of the Chinese government's United Front in 2018, according to research by Michael Lucci , a security consultant who helps protect U.S. institutions from Chinese influence through his firm, State Armor.
Cai has been photographed at several events with former Arcadia, California, Mayor Eileen Wang, who pleaded guilty to acting as a Chinese government agent in May.
"U.S.-based groups linked to the Communist Party's United Front through their key personnel keep coming up in federal foreign-agent cases," Jacqueline Deal, an adviser to State Armor, told CBS News."This is not a coincidence. The mission of these organizations is to help the Party and hurt the United States."
At a minimum, Deal said officers from these groups should have to register with the U.S. Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. That's the federal law Zhang is alleged to have violated by acting as a Chinese agent without registering as required.
Cai has not been accused of any wrongdoing or charged with any crime. He did not respond to a request for comment.
According to prosecutors, by 2025 Zhang had fully embraced a role as a Chinese government agent.
She traveled to China in January that year and met a government official and fellow graduate of the University of International Relations, the FBI affidavit said.
Two months later, the pair texted on Chinese messaging app WeChat about the address of a Taiwanese official who spoke out against the Chinese government, according to records obtained by a search warrant of Zhang's iCloud account, the FBI agent wrote.
She allegedly visited China again in June and met with a second Chinese official in the private room of a restaurant, where investigators believe she received her mission to surveil the Taiwanese president's son.
She later texted her alleged government handler: "I can take care of this thing."
After recording video of Lai and his family, she returned to LA without incident, according to the complaint. She was arrested while attempting to board a flight to Shanghai at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday.
She appeared in court on Monday dressed in the same designer workout gear she was wearing during the arrest.
Her family declined to comment.
"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, in a statement released Monday.
"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals," he said.
A spokesperson for the Taiwanese president told CBS News he condemns "such brutal acts of suppression, intimidation, and even harm to the freedom and democracy of people or their families, which are unacceptable in the civilized world."
"We thank the US judicial agency for their assistance and protection to our people," the spokesperson said. "Taiwan will continue to cooperate with all democratic allies to jointly combat illegal acts of cross-border repression."
The Chinese Foreign Ministry did not respond to CBS News' request for comment. A spokesperson  told NBC News,  "China has always opposed hyped-up accusations of 'China spying' that slander and smear the country."

articles.title_orig: Soybeans left out of U.S.-China trade talks; Minnesota farmer weighs in
articles.title_zh: Soybeans left out of U.S.-China trade talks; Minnesota farmer weighs in
articles.content_orig:
ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – Soybeans were excluded from the U.S.-China trade talks in late September. The lack of discussion on the crop was not what the American Soybean Association (ASA) hoped for.
“ASA is disappointed U.S. soybeans were not included among the agricultural products receiving additional tariff relief from China,” the organization wrote on its website. “China’s remaining 10% retaliatory duty limits access for private Chinese importers, meaning soybean trade will continue to be handled primarily by China’s state-owned enterprises. Removing the tariff would improve the competitiveness of U.S. soybeans and provide greater opportunity for private Chinese buyers.”
According to ASA, China is committed to 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans annually for 2026, 2027 and 2028.
“Any time we talk about trade in China, it’s always big news,” said Darin Johnson, who is the director of the Minnesota Soybean Growers Association. “We were a little bit let down about the lack of discussion about soybeans and trade going into the future.”
Johnson is a fourth-generation Faribault County soybean farmer. He said he was generally happy that the trade talks happened; however, it would have been ideal if the existing tariff on the agricultural product had been cut.
“The 10% tariff remains on, which is unfortunate for us as a US soybean producer,” Johnson said. “It puts us at a competitive disadvantage globally, unfortunately, especially against our biggest competitor: South America.”
KTTC spoke with University of Minnesota McKnight Professor of Applied Economics Carlisle Runge regarding the topic. He said the lack of discussion is damaging for Midwestern soybean producers.
“The Chinese want to maintain the soybean trade as leverage for further negotiations,” Runge said. “By most estimates, the trade in soybeans with China has fallen year on year anywhere from 50% to 75%.”
As a farmer, Johnson said input costs have been the main concern. He said crop prices have been better.
“We’re pretty lucky to be able to have an opportunity to be able to at least start selling some of our commodities, at least above break even at this point,” Johnson said. “Things are starting to look a little bit brighter.”
Minnesota is the third-largest state exporter of soybeans to China. Iowa and Illinois rank first and second.

articles.title_zh: Drone strike sinks ship in NATO waters as Zelenskyy warns of looming ‘massive strike’
articles.content_orig:
Drone attack sinks ship off NATO ally Bulgaria as expert warns Russia is ‘taking things up a notch’.
A commercial ship sank and its crew vanished Tuesday after an apparent coordinated air-and-sea drone attack off NATO member Bulgaria, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia before warning Moscow was preparing a broader "massive strike."
A second vessel was also heavily damaged and set ablaze inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, with a drone expert warning the dual precision strikes signaled a dangerous escalation and possible "larger invasion posture" by Russia.
"They were likely using the Geran-4 aerial drone to take the vessel out or the Maran surface vehicle to take it out," Cameron Chell, founder of drone manufacturer Draganfly , told Fox News Digital on Tuesday of the first strike.
RUSSIA MAY BE USING HIDDEN 'LUNCHBOX-SIZE' DRONE DEVICES TO COUNTER UKRAINE DEFENSES: EXPERT
The dual attack occurred roughly 70 nautical miles off the eastern Bulgarian coastal town of Byala, according to Reuters, bringing the conflict into the economic zone of a NATO member. (REUTERS/Petko Momchilov TPX IMAGES)
"The reason it wasn't just an air vehicle or an air drone that took this ship out was that the Gerans generally come in at a pretty steep angle when they're on final attack," Chell said.
"There are not really any precision drones that fly closely above the surface, which is where they would have had to hit in order to create an impact that would sink this ship fast enough," he added.
"The nature of this strike suggests there was a combination of an air attack and surface attack," Chell said.
The dual attack occurred roughly 70 nautical miles off the eastern Bulgarian coastal town of Byala, according to Reuters , bringing the conflict into the economic zone of a NATO member.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence and security services were working to determine the full circumstances surrounding the attack.

"Our intelligence and special services are now working to establish all available information about yet another attack in the Black Sea targeting civilian vessels," he wrote on X.
"Our Navy contacted its counterparts in Bulgaria, and it has been established that this was a combined Russian attack using maritime and aerial drones."
Chell suggested the attack’s location and hybrid nature could serve Russia by sowing greater uncertainty across the region.
"We can see the amount of geopolitical chaos that's involved, and this is exactly the type of thing that would benefit Russia in the region," Chell said.
"The hybrid element here is really blurring the lines between traditional military actions," he added, describing the attack as "an expansion of strategy and tactics."
"This is indicative of this larger invasion posture that seems to be unfolding for Russia," Chell said. "And a real desire, what appears to be, for Russia to take things up a notch."
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow on Sept. 5, 2026. (Gavriil GRIGOROV / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev also confirmed that aerial and maritime drones targeted two commercial vessels in shipping lanes inside Bulgaria’s EEZ , calling the attack a "gross, flagrant violation of international law," according to Reuters.
The sunken vessel, identified by British maritime risk group Vanguard as the cargo ship Alfa Watan, suffered catastrophic structural damage before submerging with an undisclosed cargo and an unknown number of crew members aboard.
A nearby Bulgarian ferry, the Dioscuria, diverted to the scene after witnessing an explosion and receiving distress signals, Reuters reported.
Rescuers found an overturned lifeboat, life rafts and life jackets floating in the debris field.
RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS
The sunken vessel, identified by British maritime risk group Vanguard as the cargo ship Alfa Watan, suffered catastrophic structural damage before submerging with an undisclosed cargo and an unknown number of crew members aboard. (YORUK ISIK/Handout via REUTERS)
Search-and-rescue operations involving the Bulgarian Navy, Air Force and Border Police remained underway to locate the missing crew and monitor for environmental threats, the outlet said.
Chell suggested the apparent coordination between the attacks was particularly significant.
"Not only are you using pretty sophisticated equipment, but you're also doing it in a coordinated manner," Chell said.
"These two ships were going opposite directions. One was actually just coming, and had left Ukraine the day before," he said.
"These things coordinated and were struck relatively at the same time. So another level of coordination has unfolded here," Chell added.
UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC
The second ship, identified by Vanguard as the general cargo vessel ABLE, caught fire after being struck while carrying grain. (Tony Hogwood/Handout via REUTERS)

A Bulgarian ferry crew evacuated all 18 seafarers aboard — 11 Turkish nationals and seven Indian nationals.
Two crew members suffered severe injuries and were airlifted to a medical facility in Varna, while the remaining 16 were transported safely to shore.
Radev convened an emergency government session following the strikes. While acknowledging it remained unclear whether the drones originated from Russia or Ukraine, he warned of the widening scope of the war.
"Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," Radev told reporters.
REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES
Search-and-rescue operations involving the Bulgarian Navy, Air Force and Border Police remained underway to locate the missing crew and monitor for environmental threats, the outlet said. (REUTERS/Petko Momchilov TPX IMAGES )
"If this war is not ended in time, it will continue to expand its spatial scope and increase the risk of even a global conflict."
Chell said striking the two ships inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone could also have the effect of disrupting a crucial shipping corridor and creating fear among commercial operators.
"It all adds up to a perfect little scenario for the Russians to create chaos there, not just to disrupt the lane of economics for the region and in particular for Ukraine — a lifeline," Chell said.
"The Russians are really taking a playbook out of the Iranians who have basically created enough chaos in the Strait of Hormuz where the operators can't take the chance to put their ships through there," he added.
The strikes came amid a surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident off Romania’s coast Monday in which two people died in a ship fire.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 rose to an all-time intraday on Tuesday, touching 7844.52 and surpassing its August 13 intraday peak when it hit 7,830. The benchmark also closed for the first time over 7,800.
The recovery comes after months of oil shocks, rising borrowing costs and the possible start of a Federal Reserve rate hiking cycle.
The record rally comes just a day after the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5.3%, reaching levels not seen since 2002. In mid September, the Fed raised its benchmark rate for the first time in over three years and indicated more were to come.
Oil had crossed $100 a barrel in early March for the first time since 2022 as the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz. After falling below $70 a barrel, it slingshot back above $100 in early September.
"At the end of the day, oil and bond yields can be correlated, but so is the stock market and profits. And if the profits are there, which they have been, the stock market is going to be resilient, even if the economy is a bit more mixed," Shawn Snyder, economic strategist at Potomac Fund Management, told CNBC.
Unlike prior records this year, this latest run has been narrowly lead by a few stocks tied to the AI hype and deemed unfettered by adverse macroeconomic headwinds.
"When traders take a breather from the noise surrounding them — much of it negative in recent months — and look closer at what's happening in the markets, it becomes clear the U.S. stock market is the best place to park their money compared with other locations. It's hard to argue against the mostly positive risk-reward ratio we've seen over multiple decades," said JJ Kinahan, Cboe Global Markets senior vice president of retail and alternative investments.
The so-called Magnificent 7 namely, Nvidia , Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft and Tesla make up more than 34% of the market cap of the S&P 500 .
"When you consider that much girth among a small handful of stocks, it's apparent how much these stocks' daily movements dictate the direction of the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, both of which are in record territory again today," Kinahan said.
With tech companies investing heavily in data centers and computing infrastructure demand for chips and equipment has gone up. Earlier this year, Amazon said it expected about $200 billion in capital expenditures across its businesses in 2026, citing opportunities including AI, chips and robotics.
Investor appetite for ambitious technology bets also became evident in June, when SpaceX raised $75 billion in the largest IPO ever and began trading on June 12. The debut became another milestone where investors continued backing growth companies despite higher energy prices and borrowing costs.
Looking ahead, however, Potomac Fund Management's Snyder cautioned that the "weakening" market breadth may last longer if inflation shows no signs of easing, or if there's no clear signal that the Federal Reserve is achieving its mandate. The central bank is slated to release its minutes from the September meeting on Wednesday.
The market "can look relatively calm, but there are still things going on underneath the surface that may not be so calm," Snyder said.
Correction: The 10-year Treasury yield on Monday surpassed 5.3% to reach highs not seen since 2002. An earlier version misstated the year.

articles.title_orig: Bulgaria's leader says drone attack hits 2 commercial vessels, and Ukraine's president blames Russia
articles.title_zh: Bulgaria's leader says drone attack hits 2 commercial vessels, and Ukraine's president blames Russia
articles.content_orig:
Russian drones started to attack Ukrainian passenger trains at the end of last year
Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator.
Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier.
"The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!"
A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border , and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before.
Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train."
She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east.
In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped.
It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes.
Passengers are routinely evacuated from trains and forced to wait on the trackside until the danger has passed
Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape.
She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September.
"On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more."
An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby.
"There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said.
It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents.
"I'm not going to travel by train anymore," she says.
Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays â some brief, others that last for hours â are now commonplace.
Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed.
Anastasiia says she will no longer travel on Ukraine's railways after a drone strike near her train last month
For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge.
"We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us.
"But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority."
Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
Confronting Russia's threat of Ukraine's railways is a game of cat and mouse, says Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, CEO of Ukrzaliznytsia
"The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi.
"It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets."
According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list.
"Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said.
Watch: Why a Russian strike on train near Ukraine-Poland border could mark an escalation
Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed â appropriately enough â the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time.
On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network.
We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point.
Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away.
"Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertsovskyi said.
Some train stoppages can last hours, causing chaos for passengers across Ukraine's rail networks
The company's precautions appear to have kept casualties low. Its figures for 2026 show that eight company employees have been killed, six of them when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv.
During our visit to Iron Command, another air raid siren sounded in Kyiv. The city's main railway station, we were told, was being evacuated.
On a later visit to the busy station, we found passengers waiting outside the main entrance or sheltering in underground passageways. Over the tannoy came news of steady stream of delays.
Everyone knows the coming months could be among the most difficult yet.
With winter not far off, Ukrzaliznytsia is already figuring out how to deal with evacuations when the outside temperature can reach -20C or below and snow is lying heavy on the ground.
Along with international donors, the company is preparing winter evacuation packs, mobile shelters and bus services in areas where evacuations become too frequent.
"We might be a slightly different railway, a reinvented railway," Pertsovskyi said. "But we'll keep connecting the country, no matter what, be it winter, be it summer, no matter how hard the enemy hits us."

articles.title_orig: France shuts down nearly 900 schools as violent education protests escalate
articles.title_zh: France shuts down nearly 900 schools as violent education protests escalate
articles.content_orig:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 6,000 people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.
Authorities estimate hundreds of thousands of protesters, including students, teachers and delegates from trade unions, took to the streets on Tuesday as protests sweep the country.
In Paris, tear gas filled the air, and trash cans, school desks and chairs were set alight as riot police with shields and batons clashed with some demonstrators.
The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.
“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”
Despite their suburban beginnings, the protests are now drawing international attention. US President Donald Trump claimed Tuesday that “what’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.”
“This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.
The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.
A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.
Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).
There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”
The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.
France’s interior ministry estimated there were about 256,000 protesters out on the streets nationwide on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris. Meanwhile, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, one of the high school student unions involved in organizing the demonstrations, suggested a much larger turnout of 450,000 people across the country.
More than 400 people were detained in Tuesday’s protests, the ministry said.
Some students have called for fresh demonstrations on Thursday.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, said “extreme violence has reached the gates of our high schools and it must be condemned unequivocally.”
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 education staff have been injured during the unrest, calling it “the highest number of education staff injured in decades.” He rejected accusations that the government had ordered police to repress the protests.
He also said officials must listen to the concerns and demands of students at each school.
“That is why time will be set aside starting this week, from Wednesday, to allow each leadership team to organize a session of internal democracy within its high school,” he wrote on X.
The Education Ministry has launched an online portal where students can share their concerns and ideas for improving their education.
The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.
The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.
Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”
The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.
CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne, Lucie Lepellec, Kate Irby and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran war could end soon, claims consumer prices will 'come tumbling down'
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran war could end soon, claims consumer prices will 'come tumbling down'
articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
Vice President JD Vance said Monday that any deal with Iran would need Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than give assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance told Reuters after a campaign trip in Alaska.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity," he added.
Vance also told the outlet that Washington is uncertain about decision-making in Tehran.
"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said.
Oil prices climbed Wednesday as investors weighed supply disruptions amid storm warnings for the Gulf of America and Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported.
Brent crude futures gained 93 cents, or 0.92%, to reach $101.51 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude (WTI) rose 82 cents, or 0.92%, to $90.25.
The price increases follow warnings from U.S. forecasters that a developing weather system in the Gulf of America is expected to intensify into the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within 48 hours.
The storm’s projected path directly threatens offshore installations that account for 15% of total U.S. crude oil production and 5% of natural gas output.
The Saudi-led coalition intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis toward the Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state TV reported, according to Reuters.
The coalition said Houthi missile threats originated from the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, as well as the governorates of Saada and Amran.
The developments came amid reports of two powerful explosions in the southern port city of Aden near its international airport.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that U.S. sanctions and the maritime blockade have crippled Tehran's oil trade and pointed to the sudden resignation of Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad.
"Iran has a new oil minister," Bessent said in a post on X .
"Considering Iran has not loaded a single barrel of crude onto a vessel since Aug. 25, what is the oil minister managing?" he asked.
The comments come as Washington ramps up "Operation Economic Outcast" to drive Iranian crude exports and revenues to zero.
Qatar confirmed Tuesday that talks and its mediation efforts between the United States and Iran are ongoing, with Doha actively working to help both nations achieve meaningful diplomatic progress.
In a statement shared on X, Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of the Media and Communication Department at Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said the diplomatic push aims to build momentum "covering all issues of concern to both parties," while Qatar acts as a key mediator.
Al Hashmi emphasized resolving long-standing tensions "requires making every effort to find negotiable solutions while taking into account the concerns of all parties involved."
He added that Qatar remains committed to maintaining open channels of communication to ensure steady progress toward stability in the region.
Three Iranians have been accused of spying on two journalists in Britain to assist Iran’s intelligence service and prepare for serious violence, prosecutors said Tuesday in London.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, allegedly conducted months of surveillance of journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, Iran International reported.
Prosecutors allege Sepahvand intended to carry out serious violence, while Javadi Manesh and Noori gathered information to help others commit serious violence.
The three men, arrested in 2025, have pleaded not guilty to all charges. They are charged under Britain’s National Security Act 2023.
President Donald Trump declared Tuesday that the United States is single-handedly carrying the burden in the conflict with Iran , arguing that global allies have left it entirely on American shoulders.
“We're into 51 years now,” Trump said, referencing the Iranian regime. “The bully of the Middle East — this should have been done a long time ago by other presidents or other countries.”
“It doesn't have to be us. It's always us. It should have been done by other countries long ago because, with time, it just got worse,” Trump said at Sparrow Point.
“But we've done a job, and frankly, I get calls all the time from the leaders of the world thanking me very much. I say, 'Good, when are you going to pay for it?' They say, 'Thank you, sir, for doing such a good job.' And I'll say to them, 'It's great — do you want to send some ships, sir?' 'I would rather not get involved.' They don't have any ships.”
“We're really holding up the whole world. It's on our shoulders, and we love doing it in a certain way,” Trump added. “We love doing it because we've gotten stronger and others have gotten weaker.”
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the U.S. is doing “extremely well” against Iran, declaring that the country’s military is “shot” and suggesting a decision is coming soon on how to bring the conflict to an end.
“We’re doing extremely well in the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said in Sparrows Point, Maryland. “They have no military. It’s shot. The whole place is shot.”
“And they were the evil one. They were the bully of the Middle East and not so much the bully anymore,” Trump said.
“But we have to finish up, and it’s only a question of which way do we want to do it: the nice way or the not-so-nice way? And pretty soon you’ll find out.”
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian dismissed talks with the United States as "meaningless" Tuesday, citing ongoing U.S. sanctions, pressure and military actions against Iran .
"Our problem with the U.S. is that every time we come to the negotiating table, war is immediately imposed upon us," Pezeshkian said after a meeting with Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan, according to the semi-official state media outlet Fars News Agency .
"Negotiations with an enemy that engages every day in assassinations, sanctions, pressure, and threats, and that violates agreements, are meaningless," he added.
"Our people do not accept such an approach either."
Pezeshkian's remarks came despite ongoing talks between Washington and Tehran, according to Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Iran’s oil minister, Mohsen Paknejad, resigned after saying the country has “no economy” and “no oil,” as Trump touted the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
“Iran is doing very poorly,” Trump told reporters ahead of traveling to Sparrows Point, Maryland.
“Their economy is gone. They have inflation of almost 300%, and their oil minister just quit,” Trump said. “He said, ‘We have no economy. We have no oil. We have nothing'.”
“The Strait of Hormuz — tremendous amounts, millions of barrels of oil — has been delivered just over the last couple of days.
“We’re getting it through at levels that we’re now, even in some times, exceeding prior to the war. We’ve done very well,” he said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian nominated sanctioned ballistic missile expert Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as defense minister on Tuesday, a move a prominent lawmaker said served as a warning to Iran’s “enemies.”
Ketabchi has roots in Iran’s missile industry and was added to a U.N. Security Council sanctions list in 2007 as head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, a Defense Ministry organization linked to Iran’s ballistic missile program.
His name returned to the U.N. sanctions list in September 2025, according to Iran International .

articles.title_orig: Crypto megadonors play it safe in the House
articles.title_zh: Crypto megadonors play it safe in the House
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency's biggest political spending network is making its first broad push into general-election House races this cycle, saying it plans to back 32 incumbents in hopes of preserving a pro-crypto bloc in Congress .
Fairshake and its affiliated super political action committees announced Monday that they have committed funds to support 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats who have supported the crypto industry's priorities.
The spending plan comes less than a month before November's midterm elections , which will determine which party controls the House and Senate.
"Fairshake has always been and always will be an issue-focused organization," spokesperson Geoff Vetter said in a statement on Monday. "We back pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties."
The network is committing at least $1 million in support of six House incumbents: Democratic Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Steven Horsford of Nevada; and Derek Tran of California; and Republicans French Hill of Arkansas , Bill Huizenga of Michigan; and Bryan Steil of Wisconsin .
Fairshake did not disclose how much the super PAC network plans to spend on the other 26 candidates.
But the network, whose backers include Coinbase, Ripple, and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz , has ample financial firepower.
Fairshake and its two affiliated super PACs, Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, entered September with about $120.4 million in cash, according to Federal Election Commission filings . Protect Progress generally supports Democrats, and Defend American Jobs generally supports Republicans.
Fairshake's network earlier this election cycle spent $71 million across 57 primaries and special elections. Its preferred candidates won 53 races.
The new general-election spending push comes weeks after the CLARITY Act , the crypto industry's signature market-structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate. That leaves the industry's biggest legislative priority unresolved, and means the next Congress could determine how crypto is regulated in the U.S.
Crypto companies back the bill because it would set clearer rules for issuing and trading tokens, shift oversight of many digital assets from the Securities and Exchange Commission to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , and reduce the risk of securities-law enforcement.
All 32 candidates whom Fairshake is backing voted for the CLARITY Act when it passed the House 294-134 in July 2025.
Several of Fairshake's biggest beneficiaries are positioned to influence how that bill is handled in the next Congress. Hill and Huizenga are, respectively, the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, while Steil leads its digital-assets subcommittee.
On the Republican side, Fairshake is backing Ben Cline in Virginia ; Troy Downing in Montana ; Tom Emmer and Michelle Fischbach in Minnesota ; Scott Fitzgerald and Bryan Steil in Wisconsin ; Mike Haridopolos in Florida ; Pat Harrigan and David Rouzer in North Carolina ; French Hill in Arkansas ; Bill Huizenga and Lisa McClain in Michigan ; Brian Jack and Austin Scott in Georgia ; Frank Lucas in Oklahoma ; August Pfluger in Texas ; Guy Reschenthaler and G.T. Thompson in Pennsylvania ; and Jason Smith in Missouri .
Its Democratic slate includes California Reps. Pete Aguilar, Jimmy Panetta and Derek Tran; Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania ; Janelle Bynum of Oregon ; Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey ; Steven Horsford of Nevada ; Jonathan Jackson of Illinois ; Lucy McBath of Georgia ; Sarah McBride of Delaware ; Hillary Scholten of Michigan ; Terri Sewell of Alabama ; and Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia .
Fairshake this cycle has already spent nearly $30 million in hopes of defeating Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown in Ohio.
Fairshake spent about $40 million to defeat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill.

articles.title_orig: French students lead massive protests against education policies
articles.title_zh: French students lead massive protests against education policies
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations.
Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
Unions, rights groups and the children have accused the authorities of using disproportionate force -- a police stun grenade tore the hand off one teenager on Monday and another youngster had his teeth knocked out last week after police fired a grenade launcher at his head.
At the Place de la Republique in central Paris, the savoury smell of grilled merguez sausages -- a French protest staple -- wafted over the crowd.
Two men in climbing gear scaled the nearby monument, where they unfurled a plastic banner reading "Neglected schools, sacrificed youth".
"Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the president would listen.
The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.
"I'm afraid for my future," Selma, 15, told AFP without giving her surname, among the thousands marching in the country's second largest city of Marseille.
The interior ministry said 86,000 had already joined demonstrations across the rest of the country earlier Tuesday. The CGT union put the figure at 260,000 people.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu responded to the demonstrations, telling lawmakers in the National Assembly that there was "no room for tolerance of violence".
"Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings," he told parliament, adding it was a "lie" to suggest the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police.
Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.
The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.
A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday.
The prosecutor's office in the northeastern town of Metz meanwhile said he called for a police inquiry over a possible sexual assault on a minor younger than 15, after video footage circulated of what appeared to be a plainclothes policeman groping a female pupil he had detained.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap.
"We just want better conditions for studying," he told AFP.
Adults turned out in droves Tuesday to support the young demonstrators.
Standing outside a school in Rennes, in western France, teacher Romain Dubourg told AFP he and colleagues had "talked about the police brutality we've witnessed" and decided to show up for the pupils.
In the eastern city of Lyon, Sandrine Buteau was among dozens of parents who organised to support the youngsters.
"As adults, we're a bit like the security cordon," she said.
Lyon teacher Rindala Younes said she was present to help the students "convey their message peacefully".
"The high school students' demands are legitimate," she said.
Amnesty International late Monday said the French authorities should "put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests".
The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry.
More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested.
The prime minister's office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured.

articles.title_orig: Russia says no plague found in contacts of Siberian lab worker who died
articles.title_zh: Russia says no plague found in contacts of Siberian lab worker who died
articles.content_orig:
Plague had not been detected among close contacts of a worker in an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia who died last week, with 60% of the identified group tested so far, officials in Russia said Tuesday.
News from Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Sunday that a female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin last week has raised public health fears worldwide.
“Laboratory testing identified two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection,” watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement, referring to the virus that causes the common cold. “No other infectious disease pathogens were detected among the contacts,” the statement said, without mentioning the word “plague.”
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he had a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the matter.
Darya Shipilova, 28, was identified by her mother and Russian media outlets as the lab worker who died.
Regional and national Russian authorities have not confirmed that plague was involved in her death. However, a State Department spokesperson said Monday there had been “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk oblast.
Separately, a State Department official told NBC News on Tuesday that the U.S. had been in contact with the Russian government as early as Friday. Health experts at the State Department had taken part in the contact along with the Russian Foreign Affairs Ministry, the official said.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also said on X that it was “working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available.”
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” it added.
The World Health Organization, which oversees global public health matters, said Tuesday that Russian health officials had informed it in response to its request about the lab worker’s death that no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk.
“According to the authorities, the woman’s illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” it said.
No case of plague or other high-threat pathogen has reportedly been found among the woman’s close contacts, the WHO said, quoting the response from the Russian officials, adding that it’s awaiting confirmation from the Russian side about “what pneumonia-causing pathogen had led to the individual’s death.”
On Friday, Maksim Modin, mayor of the Shelekhov municipal district near the border with Mongolia, said that the inpatient facility where the worker is said to have been treated had been closed for quarantine. Russian media cited officials saying that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under precautionary medical observation.
Russian media outlets have named the woman and identified her as being 28 years old. These details have not been announced by officials.
Irkutsk’s governor, Igor Kobsev, said Monday that no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body.
The Irkutsk regional branch of Rospotrebnadzor on Tuesday denied what it called “fake” reports circulating online that an “enhanced sanitary-epidemiological regime” and strict restrictions have been imposed in the region.
“No such decisions have been made at this time,” it said in a statement, saying the situation in the region remains stable.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that even though there is “very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia,” if “something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.”
Rospotrebnadzor, the health watchdog, said Tuesday its probe found “no incidents involving the handling of pathogenic microorganisms.”
Trump told reporters Monday the United States would do what it could to help Russia.
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “It’s a rough disease.”
Meanwhile, some of Russia’s neighbors have been stepping up preventive measures and quarantine controls at border crossings.
The Kremlin has called for those concerned to heed official statements.
“Rospotrebnadzor provides comprehensive information,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when reporters pressed him about rumors spreading amid sparse official statements.
Peskov also deferred to Rospotrebnadzor when asked if the worker’s lab results would be released or if an autopsy has been conducted.
On its website, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East says it was founded in 1934 “as a scientific and operational body for combating plague,” but over the years, its scope of responsibility expanded to include “other highly dangerous diseases,” including cholera and anthrax.
The institute says it’s a “multidisciplinary research and anti-epidemic facility” that helps ensure epidemic safety in the region.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he plans to speak with Putin about possible pneumonic plague case in Russia
articles.title_zh: Trump says he plans to speak with Putin about possible pneumonic plague case in Russia
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the pneumonic plague , after the death of a female staffer at a Russian anti-plague lab that’s sparked public health fears worldwide.
Asked whether he had spoken with Putin about the matter, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had a “call scheduled” and that it would take place “very soon.”
The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.
Trump had told reporters Monday that he was willing to help Russia, calling the pneumonic plague “a rough disease.”
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help.”
A Russian health watchdog said last week that Darya Shipilova, 28, a staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin.
The watchdog concluded that plague was not found among the staffer’s contacts, saying only that they found two cases of Covid and one of rhinovirus.
A State Department official told NBC News earlier Tuesday that the U.S. had been in contact with the Russian government regarding the incident since as early as Friday, following reports of Shipilova’s death.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information with the world, but asked the public not to jump to conclusions.
“Maybe, you know, there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” Rubio told reporters during a news conference in Iceland. “But I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday it was aware of and monitoring reports of the death, which it called “a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia.”
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC wrote on X .
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: School protests sweeping France cause 'heaviest toll in decades'
articles.title_zh: School protests sweeping France cause 'heaviest toll in decades'
articles.content_orig:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 6,000 people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.
Authorities estimate hundreds of thousands of protesters, including students, teachers and delegates from trade unions, took to the streets on Tuesday as protests sweep the country.
In Paris, tear gas filled the air, and trash cans, school desks and chairs were set alight as riot police with shields and batons clashed with some demonstrators.
The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.
“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”
Despite their suburban beginnings, the protests are now drawing international attention. US President Donald Trump claimed Tuesday that “what’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.”
“This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.
The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.
A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.
Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).
There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”
The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.
France’s interior ministry estimated there were about 256,000 protesters out on the streets nationwide on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris. Meanwhile, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, one of the high school student unions involved in organizing the demonstrations, suggested a much larger turnout of 450,000 people across the country.
More than 400 people were detained in Tuesday’s protests, the ministry said.
Some students have called for fresh demonstrations on Thursday.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, said “extreme violence has reached the gates of our high schools and it must be condemned unequivocally.”
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 education staff have been injured during the unrest, calling it “the highest number of education staff injured in decades.” He rejected accusations that the government had ordered police to repress the protests.
He also said officials must listen to the concerns and demands of students at each school.
“That is why time will be set aside starting this week, from Wednesday, to allow each leadership team to organize a session of internal democracy within its high school,” he wrote on X.
The Education Ministry has launched an online portal where students can share their concerns and ideas for improving their education.
The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.
The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.
Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”
The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.
CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne, Lucie Lepellec, Kate Irby and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Xbox has secured GTA 6 streaming rights
articles.title_zh: Xbox has secured GTA 6 streaming rights
articles.content_orig:
The streaming rights come in November, when Microsoft is opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming.
The streaming rights come in November, when Microsoft is opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that Microsoft is getting ready to do something around Grand Theft Auto VI that “no other platform holder is doing” during an employee all-hands this morning. According to sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans, Sharma’s brief teaser was actually about Xbox managing to land a deal for game streaming rights for Grand Theft Auto VI .
The deal will mean Xbox Cloud Gaming can stream Grand Theft Auto VI to players at launch, but it’s not clear how long the agreement will be in place. Rockstar Games still hasn’t announced a PC version of Grand Theft Auto VI , and a streaming deal would normally also allow Xbox to market its Xbox Cloud Gaming service to PC players who would otherwise need an Xbox Series X / S or PS5 console.
After The Verge originally reported that the deal would be exclusive, Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball revealed on X that Microsoft wouldn’t be streaming Grand Theft Auto VI exclusively, nor to PCs. That suggests the deal is simply for Xbox console streaming, and may mean the web browsers and apps that can usually access Xbox Cloud Gaming will not be able to stream Grand Theft Auto VI .
News of the streaming rights comes around a month after Microsoft announced some major changes to Xbox Cloud Gaming . From November, the same month Grand Theft Auto VI releases, Microsoft is limiting streaming hours to just 15 hours for Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers, 10 hours for Premium subscribers, and just five hours for Game Pass Essential.
Microsoft is also opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with a pay-as-you-go option next month, rather than being limited to Game Pass subscriptions. The pay-as-you-go option is perfectly timed for Grand Theft Auto VI , allowing those who don’t own an Xbox, or who primarily play from a phone, to stream the game by paying for a bundle of hours.
During the Xbox all-hands, Sharma also told employees that Project Helix, the next generation of Xbox hardware, will be a “family of devices” and that Microsoft will partner with others on some of those devices. Sharma first called Helix a family of devices last month in an interview, after Microsoft and AMD announced a “ strategic multi-year partnership ” last year to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console.
Correction, October 6th : Xbox has clarified that its streaming deal isn’t exclusive and Grand Theft Auto VI won’t be streamed to PCs.
