articles.title_orig: Sally Yates, former acting AG who clashed with Trump, leading Cornell assault probe
articles.title_zh: Sally Yates, former acting AG who clashed with Trump, leading Cornell assault probe
articles.content_orig:
Sally Yates, whose career in the Justice Department spanned about three decades, will lead an independent review on how Cornell University responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus, the university announced Tuesday.
The decision comes in the wake of national outrage over a former Cornell student’s allegation last month that she was gang-raped and plied with drugs at a fraternity in 2024.
New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”
The independent probe headed by Yates will look into how the university responded to those allegations and whether the school followed its policies and procedures, according to the university.
More broadly, the review will examine Cornell’s policies and practices spanning from prevention to response. It will include how reports are investigated, how disciplinary decisions are handled and how students are supported, the university said. The investigation will also look into the role and response of campus police, and its coordination with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutors. Yates did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work,” Anne Meinig Smalling, the chair of the university’s Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees, said in a statement.
An attorney for one of the Chi Phi members who was accused of sexual assault, Gillio Lopes, said they welcome the independent investigation.
“Sally Yates has tremendous experience as a prosecutor and investigator, and she and her team should have access to the full record and the freedom to follow the facts wherever they lead,” attorney Andrew Miltenberg said.
Lopes denies sexually assaulting the former student and disagreed with the Title IX finding, he said. Attorneys for several of the other men have denied wrongdoing or disputed Doe’s account.
Yates is a longtime federal prosecutor who became known in 2017 for refusing to enforce President Donald Trump’s ban on travelers to the U.S. from predominantly Muslim countries. Currently a partner at the law firm King & Spalding, she also previously investigated allegations of abuse and misconduct at U.S. Soccer.
Yates was named the deputy U.S. attorney general, the second-highest-ranking in the Justice Department, with bipartisan support in 2015. During that tenure under former President Barack Obama, Yates wrote a memo directing prosecutors to focus on individual wrongdoers in corporate cases. The memo followed the fallout of the 2008 financial crisis, in which corporations were forced to pay fines but many individual executives were not prosecuted.
Yates was also the acting U.S. attorney general for 10 days in 2017 before she was fired for refusing to defend Trump’s travel ban . Trump’s order created an early flashpoint of protest against his aggressive immigration policies.
The White House said at the time that Yates had “betrayed the Department of Justice by refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States.” The statement added that “Ms. Yates is an Obama Administration appointee who is weak on borders and very weak on illegal immigration.”
Yates wrote an op-ed in The New York Times in July 2017, after her firing, writing that Trump was “attempting to dismantle the rule of law, destroy the time-honored independence of the Justice Department, and undermine the career men and women who are devoted to seeking justice day in and day out, regardless of which political party is in power.”
“If we are not careful, when we wake up from the Trump presidency, our justice system may be broken beyond recognition,” she wrote.
Yates began her career in the DOJ in 1989 at the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia, where she was an assistant U.S. attorney. That office covers 46 counties and includes Atlanta. In 2010, Obama appointed her to lead the office, making her the first woman to do so.
She has also previously led investigations into sexual misconduct.
In 2022, Yates led an independent probe into U.S. Soccer that resulted in a damning report.
“Our investigation over the past year has revealed a league in which abuse was systematic. Verbal and emotional abuse and sexual misconduct occurred at multiple teams, was perpetrated by several coaches and affected many players,” she said at the time.
U.S. Soccer said that the findings were “heartbreaking and deeply troubling” and that it would work to thoroughly address the recommendations.
“The abuse described is inexcusable and has no place on any playing field, in any training facility or workplace,” U.S. Soccer President and former U.S. Women’s National Team member Cindy Parlow Cone said at the time.
In Cornell’s announcement on Monday, it said that Yates and her team have been asked to “examine Cornell’s overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer.”
The university said it would share the results of the review, along with any recommendations, with the Cornell community.
Daniella Silva is a national reporter for NBC News, focusing on immigration.

articles.title_orig: Sheen effect, innovative storytelling and ‘renewed energy’ mark World Mission Sunday at 100
articles.title_zh: Sheen effect, innovative storytelling and ‘renewed energy’ mark World Mission Sunday at 100
articles.content_orig:
(OSV News) — Catholics around the world will mark World Mission Sunday on Oct. 18, and a “renewed energy” infuses the annual celebration of the Church’s missionary activity this milestone year, one expert told OSV News.
“There are more and more dioceses around the country that are finding innovative ways to tell the stories of missionaries, and the need to support missionaries, the need to pray for missionaries,” said Father Anthony D. Andreassi , a priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri in Brooklyn, New York, and a researcher for the Pontifical Mission Societies USA.
Pope Leo XIV has chosen the theme “ One in Christ, united in mission ” for this year’s celebration, with his message for the day encouraging “the whole Church to continue its missionary journey with joy and zeal in the Holy Spirit.”
Established by Pope Pius XI in 1926 and universally observed by 1927, World Mission Sunday is a dedicated day of “prayer and missionary promotion throughout the Catholic world,” according to its founding decree.
Masses celebrated on the observance, which takes place on the next-to-last Sunday in October, are offered for the Church’s missions, with priests encouraged to preach homilies “of a missionary nature,” the decree states.
Father Andreassi explained the date was chosen with an eye to the feast of Christ the King (an observance also created by Pope Pius XI), which was initially celebrated on the last Sunday of October, ahead of All Saints’ Day, to underscore the Church’s missionary task ahead of Christ’s return. (Later, Pope Paul VI sought to highlight the eschatological dimensions of the Christ the King feast by making it the final Sunday of the liturgical year, immediately before the First Sunday of Advent.)
At first, the collection for World Mission Sunday was taken up in January, connecting the donations with the gifts brought by the Magi at Epiphany, said Father Andreassi, noting the mission collection was later moved to the actual observance in October.
Donations to the collection serve as the primary financial support for the Pontifical Mission Societies, a worldwide network operating at the service of the pope and consisting of four organizations designated as pontifical by Pope Pius XI in 1922.
The Society for the Propagation of the Faith supports the evangelization efforts of the local church; the Missionary Childhood Association educates children about their part in the church’s missionary outreach; the Society of St. Peter the Apostle trains the next generation of missionary clergy and consecrated religious; and the Pontifical Missionary Union focuses on forming clergy, religious and pastoral leaders more deeply in their role as evangelizers.
In 2025, donations from Catholics in the U.S. alone enabled the societies to provide more than $30 million to build churches, convents, orphanages and schools; fund catechetical projects; and support dioceses, seminarians, and men and women religious.
With 1,130 mission territories worldwide, “each gets a relatively small amount of money” through a “very collaborative process” of allocation, said Father Andreassi.
And, he said, “Even in the mission lands, even if they may be a recipient (of mission funds), they take up a collection.”
World Mission Sunday is “very much seen” as a day of “solidarity,” one on which the Church recognizes that “we are all in this together,” said Father Andreassi.
In contrast to that message of solidarity, World Mission Sunday surprisingly traces its roots in part to one of the most devastating conflicts in human history: the First World War.
That war “had dealt a serious blow to the missions, reducing the number of missionaries and disrupting many of the schools, hospitals, and charitable institutions they maintained,” Father Andreassi told OSV News, quoting from his original research on the history of World Mission Sunday.
In his 1919 apostolic letter “ Maximum Illud, ” Pope Benedict XV urged the Church to “rebuild and reinvigorate its missionary efforts,” said Father Andreassi.
But after a war that felled no less than four empires — Austro-Hungarian, German, Ottoman and Russian — Pope Benedict XV realized “you don’t just go back to doing what you used to be doing,” Father Andreassi said.
Instead, the pope placed “renewed emphasis — and in some places, emphasis for the first time — on growing a native clergy (in various nations), so that all the priests were not just from the Netherlands and England and Ireland,” Father Andreassi said.
In so doing, Pope Benedict strove to “free Catholic missionary activity from excessive identification with European nationalism and colonial interests,” said the priest. “At the same time, he sought to enlist the entire Catholic world in the missionary enterprise through prayer, missionary vocations, and financial support.”
Those efforts “exploded” when then-Msgr. — later Bishop, and now Blessed — Fulton J. Sheen was appointed the U.S. director of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith in 1950, said Father Andreassi.
A pioneer in Catholic communications with an already developed national audience, Blessed Sheen was able to place his popularity in service of the missions, said the priest.
“Now you’re starting to see Sheen on local television stations talking about World Mission Sunday,” said Father Andreassi. “You’re seeing offers in anticipation of World Mission Sunday —  if you send a few dollars to the national office, you’ll get a World Mission Rosary. So now World Mission Sunday is now becoming a huge event. There were a lot of things happening (on behalf of the missions), but he brought them up ten levels.”
The impact of Blessed Sheen “then had ripple effects on the diocesan offices” of the mission societies, the priest added.
Ahead of this year’s World Mission Sunday, the Pontifical Mission Societies have garnered increased attention with the recent beatification of the prelate in St. Louis.
Father Andreassi noted that as Blessed Sheen expanded the profile of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith during his 16-year tenure as national director, the Church was invigorating the mission field throughout the latter 20th century by sending priests to minister in other nations and to help animate local vocations.
He cited the Fidei Donum (“gift of faith”) priests, diocesan clergy assigned to foreign missions.
“Historically, if you became a priest of the Diocese of Pittsburgh, you were going to work in Pittsburgh, with some rare exceptions,” said Father Andreassi, noting that while “many religious orders already had a missionary arm to them,” the commitment of diocesan clergy to missions marked a shift.
Other inflection points in more recent years have included the COVID-19 pandemic, after which “national and the diocesan offices have really been tapping into new media to get the word out like it’s never been done before,” he said.
Another challenge is simply “trying to get the attention of Catholics,” since “so many things are pulling at our attention,” Father Andreassi said.
But missionary outreach is “central to the life of the Christian,” even in places where the Church is seemingly well grounded — including the U.S., where “many things” still “challenge or threaten the faith,” he said.
Missionary efforts must “lead to an interior transformation,” said Father Andreassi. “We’re looking to convert hearts and minds.”
Gina Christian is a multimedia reporter for OSV News. Follow her on X @GinaJesseReina .

articles.title_orig: Experts call for more complete understanding of China
articles.title_zh: Experts call for more complete understanding of China
articles.content_orig:
By XING YI in London | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-10-07 06:02
China's peaceful rise, its contribution to the Global South, and its vision of a shared future for humanity deserve to be better understood and promoted in the West, experts and activists said at the third annual Socialist China Conference in London on the weekend.
Organized by the Friends of Socialist China platform, the gathering brought together speakers from left-wing and anti-war groups in the United Kingdom and Europe, as well as representatives from embassies and academia.
Experts attending the event recalled the journey of Chinese modernization and agreed that, no matter how far China develops, the nation will continue to provide the world with development opportunities, safeguard world peace, and contribute to improving global governance.
Acknowledging the difficulties in telling the true story of China in the West, they highlighted the importance of perseverance, calling for persistent and unremitting efforts in that regard.
Carlos Martinez, co-founder of the Friends of Socialist China, said: "China is blazing a trail of modernization from outside the framework of imperialism, and China's progress is proof that socialism with Chinese characteristics is an entirely viable and highly successful model."
The conference featured three panels. During a discussion on artificial intelligence and technology, speakers compared China's approach to AI, which they said puts people at the center and promotes industrial development and open-source collaboration, with that of the United States, which they described as more closed and aimed at advancing US interests and dominance.
During the panel discussion on a multipolar world, scholars and activists from Latin America and Africa argued that China's foreign policy and infrastructure projects bring long-term benefits to their regions. They also praised China's global initiatives for emphasizing sovereign equality and multilateralism, in contrast to the rising trend of unilateralism in the US and protectionism in the West.
Resisting a new Cold War was the focus of the third panel discussion, where anti-war campaigners warned about the expansion of military alliances, including AUKUS and NATO, and stressed the need to move beyond ideological differences and to oppose imperialists' military expansion and their drive toward war.
The book China's Foreign Policy and the Making of a Multipolar World: Changes Unseen in a Century , which was edited by Keith Bennett and Carlos Martinez, co-founders of Friends of Socialist China, was also launched at the conference.
Bennett spoke about public opinion and noted that, with the US and Israel involved in conflicts in Iran and Gaza, a new generation of people has become involved in anti-war politics.
"We hope our book can reach them in explaining the theoretical underpinnings of Chinese foreign policy. We have aimed to highlight continuity amidst change and development," he said.
More than 120 people attended the conference, which was supported by the Morning Star, the Communist Party of Britain, the Workers Party of Britain, the Communist Party of Ireland, Caribbean Labour Solidarity, No Cold War Britain, the International Manifesto Group, the Black Liberation Alliance and others.

articles.title_orig: After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
articles.title_zh: After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
articles.content_orig:
Beijing is building a financial safety net around the yuan while reducing exposure to US Treasuries – a strategy that could draw increasing scrutiny from Washington
As President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump talked tariffs, agricultural quotas and critical minerals at last month’s closely watched summit in Washington, an “elephant in the room” loomed over the discussion: China’s efforts to gradually diversify away from US dollar assets.
Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific.
Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade.
“Unlike tariffs, which can be set out as part of a policy framework, sovereign debt management involves actual capital allocation and is highly sensitive, making it unlikely to be formally addressed in official statements,” Chang noted.

articles.title_orig: US seeks US$100 million bail for Chinese-born couple in surrogacy abuse case
articles.title_zh: US seeks US$100 million bail for Chinese-born couple in surrogacy abuse case
articles.content_orig:
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang allegedly had nannies beat children at their California mansion and watched on surveillance cameras
Los Angeles County prosecutors are seeking bail of US$100 million each for a Chinese-born couple charged on Tuesday with conspiring to abuse young children who were born through surrogacy and raised in their California mansion.
Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, allegedly directed nannies to physically punish the children, watched the beatings through an extensive surveillance system and coached children before police arrived to deny the abuse, according to a felony complaint.
At least 14 surrogate-born children, some as young as two months old, were abused, the district attorney’s office said. It said the couple were accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in the home to repeated physical abuse.
“The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: LG Making Doorbell, Lock, and Cameras for Apple's Home Hub
articles.title_zh: LG Making Doorbell, Lock, and Cameras for Apple's Home Hub
articles.content_orig:
Apple is working with LG Electronics on smart home accessories that will integrate with the upcoming home hub and other Apple home products, reports Bloomberg .
LG is making a wired video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt lock, temperature sensor, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and floodlight camera, according to documents LG submitted to the Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions. Apple is not mentioned in the filings, and LG asked the FCC to keep details confidential. The devices will be built and branded by LG, though Bloomberg says Apple helped develop them.
This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products' design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.
While Apple is expected to introduce the rumored home hub, a new Apple TV 4K, and a new HomePod mini on October 13, the LG accessories won't be ready to launch for a few months.
Several of LG's devices support Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Matter, with the lock also offering UWB support for close-proximity auto-unlocking.
Apple has worked with LG frequently. It uses LG Display components in its devices, and when Apple didn't sell Apple-branded displays, it teamed up with LG for 4K and 5K UltraFine monitors made for Macs. LG is not known for smart home accessories, but it bought a majority stake in smart home platform Homey in 2024. LG may be aiming to compete with Samsung SmartThings, Amazon Ring, Google Nest, and other smart home brands.

articles.title_orig: President announces submarine shipyard plan in Sparrows Point
articles.title_zh: President announces submarine shipyard plan in Sparrows Point
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump visited Maryland on Tuesday to announce a project that's expected to support 14,000 jobs and become the state's largest job creator in over a decade.
The president toured Tradepoint Atlantic with Anduril Industries, a defense technology firm in Sparrows Point, and announced that the former Bethlehem Steel site will be turned into a 2-million-square-foot shipyard to build components for Virginia-class attack submarines.
According to a media briefing, the components include torpedo tubes, sterns and bow sections, and will be built at the Sparrows Point site. Anduril said it will use advanced manufacturing and software to build submarine components and large assemblies at Sparrows Point and send them to the Navy's two main submarine builders for final assembly.
"In a tremendous victory for our country and for the city of Baltimore," Trump said. "Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in a state-of-the-art shipyard that will be known forever as Arsenal-2. It's one of the biggest and one of the most significant shipyards anywhere in the world and will be as significant as any."
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said this will be the largest private investment in the state in more than a decade. The Navy contract is worth up to $2.9 billion, while Anduril is putting in $3.7 billion of private investment — the largest single private investment in Maryland.
"With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs," said Moore. "We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we're ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together."
Raw video below: President's remarks
The facility is expected to support 14,000 jobs, including the creation of 3,100 permanent jobs. Over a decade, Arsenal-2, the name of the new industrial base, will become the state's largest job creator.
"For generations, this site shaped America's steel and shipbuilding legacy, including its critical role during World War II, when workers here built the vessels that helped defend our nation," Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier said in a statement.
The company said site preparation and permitting will begin immediately, and construction will start after the necessary approvals with initial operations expected in 2030. The timeline leaves several years to build the facility and train the workforce.
Happening right now, @realDonaldTrump has taken the stage in Sparrows Point to officially announce @anduriltech ’s new shipyard to help create the next generation of submarines for the @USNavy ! @wbaltv11 pic.twitter.com/EhDT4ohBt2
"With Arsenal-2, Anduril will return large-scale shipbuilding to a site that can once again define American naval power. This facility will make Baltimore County a critical part of America's submarine industrial base, adding the production capacity that the Navy needs to meet its Virginia-class requirements," said Brian Schimpf, Anduril cofounder and CEO.
Under the agreement, the state and Baltimore County will match up to 13% of the anticipated investment through existing economic incentive programs and new appropriations.
The state would also support the construction of a workforce training facility near Tradepoint Atlantic. Anduril said it's already developing manufacturing methods and training workers at a facility in California.

articles.title_orig: Semiconductor imports and exports have been rising all year
articles.title_zh: Semiconductor imports and exports have been rising all year
articles.content_orig:
Even imported chips can generate income here in the U.S. because many chips are designed here.
Exports have been rising steadily all year for semiconductors, which were one of the top categories of goods exports in August, according to the latest Commerce Department trade report. At the same time, we also imported more semiconductors — both for the month and year-to-date.
Semiconductors are used in the grid, data centers, your car — they’re pretty much the guts of most electronic devices.
“When you press the button to roll up your window, there's a semiconductor that tells it not to pinch your finger,” said Nina Turner, an analyst with IDC.
IDC estimates about 10% of the world’s semiconductors are manufactured in the U.S. That includes specialty chips used in cars and communications, along with certain types of memory chips — those in particular have gotten more expensive in the past year.
The U.S. has also made exporting chips a priority.
“Semiconductor companies have announced literally billions of dollars worth of investments in the last few years in manufacturing capability in the United States, and the spark for that really was the Chips and Science Act ,” said Jason Oxman, head of the Information Technology Industry Council, a trade group. (That’s the 2022 law that poured tens of billions into chip manufacturing.)
To be clear, we still import a whole lot more semiconductors than we export, but even many of those have their roots in the U.S.
“So, if you only look at who manufactures a chip and which country that chip comes from, you miss all of the complexity in the value chain,” said Chris Miller, author of the book “Chip War,” who also advises semiconductor startups. “You often miss the answers to who makes the most money per chip.”
He said almost all of the world's leading chip designers are in the U.S.
“Often, the majority of the profit accrues to the design firm rather than to the companies that actually do the manufacturing of that chip,” he said.
And for chips made overseas, that profit comes from an exported service.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he is weighing suspension of federal gas tax
articles.title_zh: Trump says he is weighing suspension of federal gas tax
articles.content_orig:
President floats idea as voter anger over rising costs threatens Republican hopes in November midterms
Donald Trump said on Tuesday his administration was considering suspending the federal gasoline tax, a sign the president is noticing voter anger over fuel costs a month before the midterm elections.
“We’re thinking about that,” Trump said when asked whether the tax should be suspended.
Any suspension would require an act of Congress. The president cannot unilaterally suspend the federal tax.
Trump first raised the idea in May, as the Iran war pushed fuel prices sharply higher. Pump prices have stayed high since. The national average for regular was $4.3685 a gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA , more than a dollar above where it stood a year ago.
The federal tax is 18.4¢ a gallon on gasoline and 24.4¢ on diesel. Dropping it would cut about 4% from the price of a gallon of regular. The tax also brings in more than $23bn a year for highways and public transit.
Asked about the midterms, Trump said he expected Republicans to “do very well”. He said his rallies, were “changing things around” because voters were hearing “what the Republicans have done”.
“Prices are now coming way down,” he said. “And oil, as soon as the war is over, which will be soon, will be coming way down.”
He gave no date for the end of the war and did not say how a tax suspension would pass Congress.

articles.title_orig: New Maryland defense shipyard gets $6.6 billion commitment and Trump visit
articles.title_zh: New Maryland defense shipyard gets $6.6 billion commitment and Trump visit
articles.content_orig:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said he was removed from the list of speakers at a White House event Tuesday at Baltimore County's Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center, where a major private investment was announced.
President Trump traveled to Tradepoint Atlantic on Tuesday to address Anduril Industries' plans for a two-million-square-foot, software-defined shipyard in Baltimore County.
The facility, known as Arsenal-2, is expected to expand America's submarine industrial base.
The State of Maryland and Baltimore County announced that the $3.7 billion private investment by Anduril is expected to create more than 3,100 permanent jobs.
Arsenal-2 will be built at Tradepoint Atlantic within the Sparrows Point complex. The project is expected to generate more than $2 billion in annual economic output, including an estimated $312 million in wages each year, according to the governor's office.
"This massive new project will deliver the largest private investment and create the most jobs in Maryland in over a decade—driving billions of dollars in economic activity that will boost Maryland families not just in Baltimore County, but throughout the state," Moore said. "With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs. We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we're ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together."
Moore was initially scheduled to speak at Tuesday's event alongside Trump but was removed from the program after the White House objected to his inclusion Monday.
Moore confirmed Tuesday that he would no longer attend the event after recording a debate with Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox.
"If the President of the United States wants to bring the circus to town and tell me that I am not allowed to speak to the fact that we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted  while I go back to the people of Maryland," Moore said.
The White House told CBS News Baltimore that Moore was invited to attend the event as a guest.
"President Trump is willing to work with anyone to revitalize our manufacturing sector, which is why the White House graciously invited Governor Moore to attend today's event as a guest," a White House spokesperson stated. "It's unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion-dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump."
A spokesperson for the governor's office added, "Governor Moore has always said he will work with anyone when it comes to delivering for Marylanders but bow to no one when it comes to standing up for them. The Governor is proud to welcome Anduril to Baltimore County and the thousands of permanent jobs this investment is bringing to our state."
Rep. Johnny Olszewski, a former Baltimore County executive and current Maryland congressman, was among the Democratic lawmakers who chose not to attend the event after Moore was removed as a speaker, according to The Baltimore Banner.
Olszewski told The Banner in a statement that the focus should remain on the investment coming to Baltimore County.
"I proudly support all efforts to continue providing new opportunities for future generations," Olszewski said.
Baltimore County Councilman and county executive candidate Julian Jones also chose not to attend.
Moore and Trump have clashed on issues including the Francis Scott Key Bridge rebuild, redistricting, crime and immigration enforcement.
Last week, Moore told CBS News Baltimore that he would invite Trump to join him on a boat tour of the Francis Scott Key Bridge reconstruction site.
"I would love it if the president were to choose to join me at that, so he could see the unprecedented speed and unprecedented progress that's happening with this rebuild," Moore said.
CBS News Baltimore reached out to the White House for comment but has not heard back.
In 2025, Moore invited Trump to visit Maryland and participate in a public safety walk after the National Guard was deployed in Washington, D.C.
The White House responded by pointing to Baltimore's crime rate.
A White House spokesperson said, "Perhaps Gov. Moore should take a page out of the President's playbook."
At the time, the White House also said Baltimore was the fourth-most-dangerous city in the United States.
According to a U.S. News & World Report ranking, Baltimore ranked behind Memphis, Oakland and St. Louis.
In February 2026, Moore said he was singled out and excluded from a couple of bipartisan events for the nation's governors.
Moore said the president excluded him from a dinner for governors and their spouses for National Governors Association (NGA) in Washington, D.C., along with Colorado Gov. Jared Polis.
Moore, the vice chair of the NGA, attended the annual NGA meeting after he said the White House reinvited him.
"I will attend today's business meeting with my colleagues at the White House," Moore said. "But let me be abundantly clear: I will not participate in political stunts."

articles.title_orig: Trump blames mass protests in France on ‘out of control mass migration’ and Islam
articles.title_zh: Trump blames mass protests in France on ‘out of control mass migration’ and Islam
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations.
Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
Unions, rights groups and the children have accused the authorities of using disproportionate force -- a police stun grenade tore the hand off one teenager on Monday and another youngster had his teeth knocked out last week after police fired a grenade launcher at his head.
At the Place de la Republique in central Paris, the savoury smell of grilled merguez sausages -- a French protest staple -- wafted over the crowd.
Two men in climbing gear scaled the nearby monument, where they unfurled a plastic banner reading "Neglected schools, sacrificed youth".
"Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the president would listen.
The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.
"I'm afraid for my future," Selma, 15, told AFP without giving her surname, among the thousands marching in the country's second largest city of Marseille.
The interior ministry said 86,000 had already joined demonstrations across the rest of the country earlier Tuesday. The CGT union put the figure at 260,000 people.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu responded to the demonstrations, telling lawmakers in the National Assembly that there was "no room for tolerance of violence".
"Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings," he told parliament, adding it was a "lie" to suggest the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police.
Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.
The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.
A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday.
The prosecutor's office in the northeastern town of Metz meanwhile said he called for a police inquiry over a possible sexual assault on a minor younger than 15, after video footage circulated of what appeared to be a plainclothes policeman groping a female pupil he had detained.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap.
"We just want better conditions for studying," he told AFP.
Adults turned out in droves Tuesday to support the young demonstrators.
Standing outside a school in Rennes, in western France, teacher Romain Dubourg told AFP he and colleagues had "talked about the police brutality we've witnessed" and decided to show up for the pupils.
In the eastern city of Lyon, Sandrine Buteau was among dozens of parents who organised to support the youngsters.
"As adults, we're a bit like the security cordon," she said.
Lyon teacher Rindala Younes said she was present to help the students "convey their message peacefully".
"The high school students' demands are legitimate," she said.
Amnesty International late Monday said the French authorities should "put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests".
The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry.
More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested.
The prime minister's office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured.

articles.title_orig: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
articles.title_zh: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has confirmed its first ever case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years.
Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city.
Kenya's health ministry says it has since stepped up surveillance at airports and border crossings.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
Since then, all known cases of the highly infectious disease have been in DR Congo.
The virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment.
​​There are however four vaccines in development, with human trials for one of them launched in July.
Duale confirmed that the Kenyan national had tested positive for the Bundibugyo species.
According to the minister, the patient first travelled by road from DR Congo to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi.
Duale said that after being taken to the Nairobi Hospital, the patient was transferred to an isolation facility that was built during the Covid-19 pandemic.
It was there that the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin".
"Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said.
The patient died at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and he was buried on Tuesday in line with public health safety protocols.
At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, have been identified, while health authorities are tracing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight.
A senior health ministry official said the patient might have passed screening at the airport because the medication he was taking masked his symptoms.
Kenya introduced tighter checks at airports and border posts after the outbreak was declared in DR Congo but these have now been further intensified.
The health minister urged Kenyans "not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease".
He asked health workers to be "extra vigilant and maintain the highest infection prevention and control measures regardless of the condition being treated".
The WHO has recorded 4,114 deaths out of 8,544 cases in the current outbreak, making it the largest ever recorded in DR Congo, where Ebola was first discovered in 1976.
Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) believes the current toll could be even higher because of gaps in surveillance and testing in the war-torn country.
On Monday, MSF said the virus was spreading "like a megafire", with new hotspots emerging in North Kivu province, which borders Ituri where the virus began.
Since early September this had "intensified dramatically" with the province now accounting for nearly 40% of all newly confirmed cases nationwide, MSF said.
Eastern DR Congo has been riven by decades of conflict, with multiple rebel groups operating in the region amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.
The crisis has led to the death and displacement of millions of people, and  hampered the country's ability to develop and maintain functional health care systems and infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Depression 9 forms in Gulf. What does that mean for Texas?
articles.title_zh: Tropical Depression 9 forms in Gulf. What does that mean for Texas?
articles.content_orig:
HOUSTON - Texas has its eyes peeled on the southern Gulf where Tropical Depression 9 formed Tuesday.
The system, which had been designated Invest 92L, is located in the Bay of Campeche.
According to the forecast from the National Hurricane Center, Tropical Depression 9 will stay east of Texas. It is forecast to come ashore along the northern Gulf Coast later this week.
Tropical Depression 9 is forecast to become Tropical Storm Isaias by Tuesday night or Wednesday morning, and then become the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season by Thursday.
Most computer forecast models agree that Tropical Depression 9 will not be a big problem for Texas. However, anytime there is a tropical system in the Gulf, it is worth watching closely.
It doesn’t take a landfalling tropical system to cause problems for coastal Texas. With a system in the Gulf, rip currents and coastal flooding can become problems in addition to the heavy rain and gusty winds that they can bring.
The National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi has issued a coastal flood advisory for the barrier islands until 7 p.m. Tuesday. Forecasters said water could be pushed up to beach dunes on the Aransas, Kleberg, Nueces and Calhoun islands. This can lead to difficult driving and blocked roads.
Parts of the Texas coast will also see enhanced rainfall chances this weekend as the system moves toward the northern Gulf Coast, but the amounts look manageable at this time.
The Source: Information in this story came from the National Hurricane Center, the National Weather Service and FOX Weather.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government fighters shown driving vehicles over Houthi opponents
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government fighters shown driving vehicles over Houthi opponents
articles.content_orig:
Forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government have launched an operation to capture a strategic mountainous district from the Houthis as part of a wider push to retake the Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The offensive on the district of al-Waziiya in Taiz governorate on Tuesday came as Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government, intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting the city of Khamis Mushait.
The operation is part of the "Dawn of Yemen" offensive that was announced on Sunday by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.
The media centre of Yemen's army said in a post on X that the Homeland Shield Forces, a pro-government military faction, have begun "a large-scale operation" to retake al-Waziiya.
"The armed forces have secured strategic hills overlooking the al-Mansoura area, amidst a mass retreat by the Houthi militia," it said, citing a military source.
The Houthis, however, denied the claim, saying they had successfully repelled the Yemeni government advance in al-Waziiya.
The mountainous district is located west of Taiz, east of the Red Sea port of Mocha. The Houthis had seized Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a strategic maritime corridor – in a lightning offensive last month.
"These are the mountains that the Houthis took control of prior to the takeover of the city of Mocha," Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry said, reporting from Sanaa.
"If the Yemeni government is serious about taking over the city of Mocha, they cannot do so unless they take over the region in the district of al-Waziiya," he added.
The fighting came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthi missile threats originated from Houthi-held Sanaa and the governorates of Saada and Amran.
"The coalition continues to neutralise the threat posed by ballistic and surface-to-surface missiles and to destroy their launch sources," he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in Jazan and Najran airport, near the Yemen border, were hit in attacks that wounded three people.
The attacks caused injuries of "varying severity" and material damage, and the injured have been taken to hospital, the authority said.
The Houthis said late on Monday that their forces targeted sites across southern Saudi Arabia, including airports and military sites.
The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive to retake all Houthi-held territory, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support.
Pakistan and Turkiye have also agreed to activate "deterrence measures" under their mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by the Houthis.

articles.title_orig: Ravens’ Marlon Humphrey, Tyler Loop to join Trump at Sparrows Point
articles.title_zh: Ravens’ Marlon Humphrey, Tyler Loop to join Trump at Sparrows Point
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump visited Maryland on Tuesday to announce a project that's expected to support 14,000 jobs and become the state's largest job creator in over a decade.
The president toured Tradepoint Atlantic with Anduril Industries, a defense technology firm in Sparrows Point, and announced that the former Bethlehem Steel site will be turned into a 2-million-square-foot shipyard to build components for Virginia-class attack submarines.
According to a media briefing, the components include torpedo tubes, sterns and bow sections, and will be built at the Sparrows Point site.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said this will be the largest private investment in the state in more than a decade.
"With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs," said Moore. "We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we're ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together."
The facility is expected to support 14,000 jobs, including the creation of 3,100 permanent jobs. Over a decade, Arsenal-2, the name of the new industrial base, will become the state's largest job creator.
"For generations, this site shaped America's steel and shipbuilding legacy, including its critical role during World War II, when workers here built the vessels that helped defend our nation," Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier said in a statement.
The $3.7 billion private capital investment will become the largest single private investment in the state.
Happening right now, @realDonaldTrump has taken the stage in Sparrows Point to officially announce @anduriltech ’s new shipyard to help create the next generation of submarines for the @USNavy ! @wbaltv11 pic.twitter.com/EhDT4ohBt2
"With Arsenal-2, Anduril will return large-scale shipbuilding to a site that can once again define American naval power. This facility will make Baltimore County a critical part of America's submarine industrial base, adding the production capacity that the Navy needs to meet its Virginia-class requirements," said Brian Schimpf, Anduril cofounder and CEO.
Under the agreement, the state and Baltimore County will match up to 13% of the anticipated investment through existing economic incentive programs and new appropriations.
The state would also support the construction of a workforce training facility near Tradepoint Atlantic.

articles.title_orig: China Refiners Flock to Iraqi Crude
articles.title_zh: China Refiners Flock to Iraqi Crude
articles.content_orig:
China’s independent refiners are turning to Iraqi crude after a US blockade choked supplies from top source Iran, while competition from state-owned rivals priced most of them out of Russian barrels.
Private processors, including smaller ‘teapot’ refiners in Shandong province, have bought Iraq’s Basrah Heavy and Basrah Medium grades for November delivery at premiums of as much as $18 a barrel to ICE Brent, according to traders familiar with the matter. The purchases point to a rush for prompt supplies rather than a strong recovery in Chinese oil demand .
At least 50 tankers, mostly carrying Iranian crude, are bottled up along the nation’s coast as a US blockade seeks to pressure Tehran into ending the seven-month war on terms favorable to Washington. At the same time, state-owned Chinese refiners are taking most of the available Russian crude, driving up costs for independent processors.
Inventories at some Shandong teapots could run out as early as the end of this month, forcing refiners to compete for a shrinking pool of alternatives just as Beijing issued fresh crude-import quotas, said Muyu Xu, senior crude analyst at Kpler. “To avoid shutting down or significantly cutting run rates, refiners need to secure alternative supplies as soon as possible.”
The supply squeeze has pushed some processors toward sulfur-rich Basrah crude, which they typically avoid in favor of cheaper Iranian barrels and diesel-rich ESPO from Russia’s Far East.
Improving Middle Eastern flows , as Gulf producers move more oil through the Strait of Hormuz, are also making Iraqi crude increasingly accessible. Producers in the region are deepening discounts to defend market share after Saudi Aramco cut the price of its flagship grade for Asian buyers.
Meanwhile, Russian barrels remain expensive, with ESPO commanding a premium of almost $30 a barrel above Brent, the traders said, asking not to be identified as the negotiations are private.
“Teapots are very price sensitive,” Kpler’s Muyu Xu said, adding that Basrah is now cheaper than Russia’s ESPO, making those barrels increasingly attractive to private refiners.
Buyers of Iraqi crude include both private processors in China’s Shandong province and some large independent refiners, according to the traders. Iraqi barrels are typically marketed by trading houses such as Vitol Group, Trafigura Group and Mercuria Energy Group, as well as TotalEnergies SE.
Iran was a major crude supplier to China’s independent refiners before the blockade, with imports exceeding 1 million barrels a day prior to the war. Private processors were the main buyers, attracted by steep discounts on sanctioned barrels that bolstered refining margins.

Deals Tablets Smartwatches Apple Samsung Google Amazon
Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days start today and end tomorrow. We’ve already looked at the best phone deals for the US. Here we will take a look at the best tablet offers, also smartwatches and some Amazon devices.
Apple launched new iPad Airs earlier this year, an 11” and a 13” model. The one major difference between these and the 2025 versions is the Apple M4 chipset with 4 extra gigs of RAM for 12GB total. It also has faster Wi-Fi 7 connectivity and Bluetooth 6.0. Even with all this power, the Airs still use 60Hz IPS LCDs. Multitasking on an external display via Stage Manager is enabled by the USB-C 3.1 Gen2 port.
If you want something more portable, the Apple iPad mini (2024) runs on an Apple A17 Pro chipset, which enables Apple Intelligence. It has an 8.3” display (60Hz IPS LCD) and a USB-C 3.1 Gen2 port.
Samsung didn’t refresh its 11” flagship tablet, which leaves the Galaxy Tab S11 as the current model. It has a 120Hz OLED display and a Dimensity 9400+ chipset with full DeX support, both wired (over the USB-C 3.2 port) and wireless. There were no Tab S12s on offer.
The Galaxy Tab S10 FE and Tab S10 FE+ are also from last year – they have 10.9” and 13.1” IPS LCDs, respectively. Both are powered by the Exynos 1580 chipset with expandable storage. However, their USB-C ports are only USB 2.0. The smaller tablet has an 8,000mAh battery, while the larger model has a 10,090mAh battery.
The Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Lite also has a 10.9” 90Hz LCD, but it’s not an IPS panel. This one is a cheaper alternative and uses the older Exynos 1380 chip, also with expandable storage. The battery capacity is the same at 8,000mAh.
Even cheaper is the Samsung Galaxy Tab A11+. This one has a similar 11” display, a 90Hz LCD, and a smaller 7,040mAh battery. It switches to a Dimensity 7300 chipset and retains the microSD slot.
The new Apple Watch Series 12 updates the chipset over the Series 11, an S11 instead of S10, which enables the new Apple Intelligence features. Additionally, it has new biometric sensors, which allow it to read your heart rate more often.
Note that all of these watches have versions with cellular connectivity – we’ve noted the price premium for that. On the Apple Watch Series 12 this means 5G, while the others have 4G.
The Apple Watch SE 3 is still good too – it uses the older S10 chip with 64GB storage, just like the Series 10 and Series 11. There’s no ECG, but it does have the heart rate reader.
Samsung’s new Watch9 series isn’t part of the discounts, so we turn our attention to Galaxy Watch8 and Galaxy Watch8 Classic from 2025. That is still the latest model with a rotating bezel if that’s your thing. However, these use the older Exynos W1000 chip. Both have ECG.
The 4G version of the Google Pixel Watch 5 also has satellite SOS – it’s a good backup in case you lose your phone (or if your phone lacks satellite connectivity in the first place).
Amazon has discounted its Kindle Scribe e-readers by 24% – there’s a monochrome version and a Colorsoft version. These have larger 11” displays, so they are better-suited for reading documents than the typical Kindle. Also, they come bundled with a stylus in case you want to use it to take notes or sketch ideas.
The Amazon Echo Show 15 and 21 have 15” and 21” displays – they are not quite tablets and not quite TVs either, but they can function as either. These are great as control hubs for your smart home.
There are also the Amazon Echo Show 8 and 11, if you don’t care for the large, wall-mounted version. These have dual drivers and a 2.8” woofer in their bases and 8.7” or 11” displays, respectively. These can also control your smart home and they have 13MP cameras for video calls. The larger 15” and 21” models also have cameras, but it may be trickier to get the angle right, depending on where you mount them.
Amazon unveiled the Fire TV Stick 4K (2026) just last week and now it’s half off. It supports HDR10, HDR10+ and HLG (but not Dolby Vision – you want the 4K Max for that), along with the H.264, H.265, VP9 and AV1 codecs. Note that this doesn’t run the Android-based Fire OS but uses the proprietary Vega OS instead.

Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief has been detained on suspicion of passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the country’s federal prosecutor’s office has said.
Prosecutors allege August Hanning, whose tenure at the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) ended in 2005, paid for access to classified documents from a former aide at the BND. It is claimed Hanning used them to prepare an analysis which he intended to sell on to a foreign intelligence service as part of his consulting activities.
He is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason and espionage”, the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Prosecutors did not identify which foreign intelligence service he was allegedly preparing the analysis for, and it ⁠was not immediately clear whether it reached its intended recipient.
According to German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung the case does not ⁠involve Russia.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Tölz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany on Tuesday. The former aide, ‌identified only as Manfred D, was also arrested on Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany.
Manfred D is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Prosecutors said they are also searching the suspects’ premises in these locations and in Berlin.
From the spring of 2010 until July 2022, Manfred D continuously obtained valuable information for Hanning from the BND in exchange for payment, said the prosecutor’s statement.
He allegedly provided him with nearly 2,000 documents, many of them classified and intended solely for internal use within the BND and senior-level intelligence ‌briefings at the chancellery.
According to the statement, Hanning was in close contact with a member of another state intelligence service, and he supplied this individual with political information over several years, which was partly based on material he had received from Manfred D.
Hanning was president of the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. Manfred D served as his chief of staff at that time, and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
“In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor's office said.
The German newspaper Bild said that the investigation was launched after the discovery of an alleged leak of intelligence reports intended for the chancellery.
The arrests came after a separate investigation into allegations that Hanning abducted Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.
The current investigation stems from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
Both of the accused will be brought before the investigating judge of the Federal Court of Justice on Tuesday and Wednesday.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz voiced his shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
“This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
“We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations levelled against former BND chief Hanning,” von Notz told Spiegel Online.

articles.title_orig: Cornell Faculty Senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell Faculty Senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty members introduced a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house.
The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday evening, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
“That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” says the resolution, which is less than half a page.
The measure is expected to be considered by the Faculty Senate, which meets Oct. 14, Faculty Senate member Paul Ortiz said in a statement.
Ortiz said in an interview: “My primary job as an educator is to make sure my students are studying and learning in a safe environment. If they don’t feel safe, they can’t learn, they can’t study, they can’t thrive, they can’t grow as individual human beings.”
Ortiz added that there is a “climate of fear among women students.” He emphasized that the Senate’s goal is to force “systemic change” rather than advocate to have one or two people, such as university President Michael Kotlikoff, step down.
You get “rid of one person, and then you bring a new person into a dysfunctional environment,” Ortiz said.
“A lot of the students would like the president to step down, but we decided not to have that in the resolution,” he added.
In a statement accompanying the resolution, the faculty sponsors said “numerous Cornell colleagues” had approached them demanding action, while students had told faculty members they were “upset [and] fearful for their personal safety” and wanted the Ivy League school to address sexual assault on campus.
Cornell alumni had also contacted faculty members and shared “their own traumatic stories as students,” the statement said.
Cornell declined to comment.
The proposed no-confidence resolution escalates the pressure on Cornell and its administration following national scrutiny over how the case was handled. Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with her allegation of sexual assault.
She alleges that multiple fraternity members sexually assaulted her in October 2024 while she was impaired by alcohol, ketamine and marijuana.
The woman’s allegations have made national headlines for days, and they prompted protests on campus following widespread criticism that the university and local officials did not do enough to investigate them.
Anne Marie Elizabeth Brady, a Faculty Senate member and research director for the university’s Industrial and Labor Relations Workers Institute, said the resolution came together “quickly” in recent days.
“If I was a woman on Cornell’s campus, I’d run in the other direction,” she said. “Because I’m not sure Cornell is there to protect the students the way they should be.”
Brady said Cornell’s decision to discipline the seven men accused of wrongdoing instead of passing the case on to outside law enforcement “feels like a cover-up to me.”
“If I’m a betting woman, I suspect they didn’t do that because they wanted to keep it secret,” she said. “They wanted to manage the story.”
If the Faculty Senate passes the resolution, Brady said, it will then prompt a series of discussions between faculty members and Cornell’s leadership for policies about sexual assault.
Similar action was taken last year following years of campus protests of the war in Gaza. Brady said those recommendations have largely been ignored.
“If the administration came out and said: ‘You know what? We screwed up, we did A, B and C wrong. We failed this student, we failed all our students through this process and these are the concrete ways and steps we are going to take to change,’” she said, “if they did that? That goes so far.”
Adam Reiss and Maggie Vespa reported from Ithaca and Matt Lavietes from New York City.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.content_orig:
A new World War II Primary Source Set from the Library of Congress supports teachers, librarians, and students in examining the people, places, and events of the war through primary sources from the Library’s digital collections. The eighteen-source set features newspapers, photographs, posters, maps, oral histories, letters, and other materials created during the period. A background essay provides historical context, teaching ideas, and links to additional Library of Congress resources.
These sources offer opportunities to explore some of the central questions and experiences of World War II from multiple perspectives. Americans contributed to the war effort as soldiers and civilians, workers and volunteers, and community members.
We hope this new source set will both be a useful and insightful way to explore World War II through the voices, images, and experiences preserved in the Library of Congress collections, and inspire students’ further inquiry and deeper investigation.

articles.title_orig: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.title_zh: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.content_orig:
London, United Kingdom – The deadline Israel imposed on the United Kingdom to close its East Jerusalem consulate is fast approaching.
Thursday marks 30 days since Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar’s order, a retaliatory move against the UK’s wave of sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements.
“It’s not the act of a friend or ally,” Sir Vincent Fean, former British consul general to Jerusalem, told Al Jazeera. “The British Consulate General has every right to be in Jerusalem, in East Jerusalem, part of the state of Palestine.”
From 2010 until 2014, Fean held the post as the de facto ambassador to occupied Palestinian territory. He is now a trustee of the Britain Palestine Project, advocating for equal rights for Palestinians and Israelis.
“In international law, for [the UK], and for the vast majority of the world, Israel does not have the right to interfere with the diplomatic relations between the state of Palestine and the state of the United Kingdom. It is doing so by closing our office, and that is unlawful,” he said, adding that he is “particularly concerned” for the consulate’s 50 or so Palestinian staff.
UK-Israel ties have reached a nadir. On Monday, reports claimed that the UK could expel 27 Israeli diplomats if the consulate closure goes ahead.
British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell has reportedly held talks with Israeli officials in a visit that was not disclosed by the UK government, but an agreement to keep the consulate open was not reached.
Israel’s response was furious following the UK’s import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, as well as an overall change of tone. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has, for instance, lamented Israel’s “ethnic cleansing” against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Miliband expected Israel to retaliate, but said the UK had “weighed the costs and benefits of acting”.
In addition to the consulate closure order, Israel expelled the UK from the Washington-led coordination centre for post-war Gaza and barred 11 lawmakers from entering Israel, including former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana.
“It is illegal and unlawful for Israel to act in this way,” Fean told Al Jazeera. “There’s been a reset in UK foreign policy since [Prime Minister Andy] Burnham and Miliband came in.”
Israel’s hostile actions towards the UK “will not be forgiven or forgotten anytime soon”, he added.
In a brief by the Britain Palestine Project that was endorsed by former UK Attorney General Dominic Grieve KC and shared with Al Jazeera, the threatened closure is described as “an unlawful assertion of sovereignty over occupied Palestinian territory”.
“The Israeli announcement usurps the rights of the State of Palestine,” it reads.
Resolution 478 was adopted by the United Nations Security Council – of which the UK is a permanent member – in 1980, resolving that Israel’s attempts to alter the status of Jerusalem are “null and void”.
In 2016, Resolution 2334 reiterated this, “condemning all measures aimed at altering the demographic composition, character and status of the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem”.
The UK formally recognised the State of Palestine in September of 2025 .
If the UK resists Israel’s orders, there are various logistical challenges Israel could feasibly impose on the consulate and the diplomats within it.
“The practicality is that the Consulate General depends on Israeli electricity [and] water. So there are means by which Israel could force the expulsion, the closure, of the Consulate General,” Fean told Al Jazeera. “I don’t know what’s going to happen, but this Israeli government has broken many laws,” he said when asked if Israel may use electricity or water cut-offs as a means to expel British diplomats.
While reiterating that the UK’s East Jerusalem consulate should remain open despite orders, Fean said that “if that proves to be made impossible by force of the Israeli government, then there are alternatives.”
Foreign embassies in Ramallah could be an alternate route to manage consulate affairs, he said.
The consulate acts as the channel of communications between the UK and the Palestinian government and manages consular affairs for British nationals in the region, including pilgrims to the West Bank.
“Yet again, Israel is taking it out on the Palestinians for something that somebody else has done,” said Fean. “The impunity of Israel needs to be challenged. The fact that this Israeli government seems to see itself as above the law needs to be challenged.”
Human rights advocates have urged the UK to resist Israel’s orders.
“Such a retaliatory step from Israel suggests that any further measures taken by the UK could trigger further responses,” said Zena Agha, deputy director of the British Palestinian Committee. “But that should not deter the UK from meeting its obligations under international law – nor pursuing measures towards accountability for Israel’s genocide and occupation.”
Shamiul Joarder, director of Friends of al-Aqsa, reiterated the illegality of Israel’s actions and told Al Jazeera, “If Britain accepts this order, it risks allowing Israel to dictate the terms of Britain’s diplomatic presence in occupied East Jerusalem. That would set a deeply concerning precedent.”
The Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on Israel’s orders to close the British Consulate, nor on the UK’s intended response.
