articles.title_orig: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.title_zh: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.content_orig:
Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director at Chanel . “I am happy with where we are at.”
Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. In Vanity Fair’s list of the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.
Blazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.
One of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featured Vanessa Paradis in a birdcage ; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.
After several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.
The same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.
after newsletter promotion
On his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”
The famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.

articles.title_orig: Google launches Nano Banana 2.1 with better editing and subject consistency
articles.title_zh: Google launches Nano Banana 2.1 with better editing and subject consistency
articles.content_orig:
Google has released Nano Banana 2.1, a new model for image generation and editing.
It replaces Nano Banana 2 , released in February 2026, and Google says it improves on previous versions "across the board." Nano Banana Pro likely remains Google's best image model, but it uses the most recent Pro model, 3.1, while 2.1 uses Gemini 3.6 Flash . The next major gain in image quality could come with Google's announced Pro model, Gemini 4 Argon .
Google is also cutting prices roughly in half compared with Nano Banana 2. A 1K image costs 3.36 cents, down from 6.70 cents, while a 4K image drops from 15.10 to 7.56 cents. Nano Banana Pro costs considerably more at 13.40 cents per 1K image.
According to Google , version 2.1 improves visual quality, text rendering, character consistency across conversation turns, wide panoramas, and infographics. It can process up to 14 reference images at once, keeping up to four characters and ten objects consistent. The model also connects to Google Search and offers minimal, medium, and high thinking levels that affect image quality.
Although 2.1 sometimes beats Pro by a wide margin in benchmarks, Nano Banana 2 also matched it in those tests. In practice, Nano Banana Pro often still produces noticeably better images. Google describes 2.1 as "the more efficient counterpart" to Pro.
The model runs at Flash-tier speed, supports 1K, 2K, and 4K resolutions, and is already rolling out across Google's products. These include the Gemini app, AI Mode in Google Search, Google AI Studio, Flow by Google, Stitch by Google, Google Ads, and the Gemini Enterprise Platform.
More details are available in the model card . Google will shut down the previous model , "gemini-3.1-flash-image," on October 29, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Europe’s moment of supreme confidence
articles.title_zh: Europe’s moment of supreme confidence
articles.content_orig:
As global alliances shift and economic competition intensifies, Europe is responding with deeper integration, large-scale investment and renewed confidence in its industrial and technological strengths
If there is one key takeaway from the recent Munich Security Conference, it is a message of trust and confidence in Europe. The EU is a technology, trade and industry powerhouse. Around Europe, the signs of this strength abound: off the northern coast of Poland, just beyond the horizon, 233 giant turbines – each almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower – are about to rise from the sea floor. With German rotors, foundations designed in Denmark, and cables from Poland and Greece, they will be towering symbols of European manufacturing excellence and industrial might. As the latest additions to an already vast Baltic fleet, they are creating thousands of jobs across the supply chain; and when they are operational, they will supply an additional 5.5 million households with clean energy.
Producing energy made in Europe, by Europe, for Europe, Poland’s offshore wind farms are as important strategically as they are economically. They add to a buildout of clean power that is happening across the continent from Italy in the South to Ireland and Lithuania in the North. Cables and interconnectors – enough to wrap the Earth many times over – are being laid to link the windy northern seas with the sunlit Mediterranean coastline, creating a superhighway for the age of electrons.
An investment revolution is underway Meanwhile, cutting-edge fibre-optic sensors pioneered by Dutch innovators will be watching over the seabed to protect Europe’s critical infrastructure. New constellations of satellites developed in Belgium will offer enhanced surveillance capabilities from space, alongside cutting-edge radar systems from France and Spain. And all these systems will be connected by AI-powered 6G networks developed in Finland.
These are just a few of the nearly 900 investment projects financed by the European Investment Bank Group last year alone ( see Fig 1 ). By leveraging EU budget guarantees to mobilise private investment, the EIB Group is powering the unfolding energy and technological revolutions. The transition into tomorrow’s world is already in full swing in Europe – a major development that remains overlooked amid rapid geopolitical change. In fact, the overall investment in the EU’s energy transition reached a new record in 2025, approaching €400bn – from hydropower in Austria to new railways in Czechia, and from energy efficiency upgrades by small businesses in Croatia to clean technologies deployed by heavy industries in Portugal. Just in the past year, the combined market capitalisation of European renewables companies has risen by over 50 percent. Something that many thought impossible in the near term is already happening – Europe is irreversibly weaning itself off Russian gas.
European investments in defence are increasing even more rapidly. European defence stocks have tripled in value in the past three years. Europe’s industrial production capacity now exceeds even that of the US in critical areas, including artillery shells. Europe is moving by leaps and bounds into strategic sectors and technologies such as drones.
A new venture-capital ecosystem geared toward pioneering security and defence enterprises has emerged almost overnight and essentially from scratch.
A continent reshaped by disruption We have seen a similar mobilisation before. In 2020, no one expected that a European biotech company would pioneer a vaccine against an unknown virus in a matter of months, helping the world defeat a once-in-a-century pandemic. Nor did anyone think that European leaders would launch a massive recovery and resilience programme financed by joint debt – an unprecedented show of solidarity and unity. When Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine caused a massive spike in energy prices, everyone assumed that the European economy would buckle. Instead, the eurozone’s GDP grew faster than China and the US that year.
In the face of trade warfare, intense market volatility, and shifting traditional partnerships and alliances, European companies have proven resilient, not only diversifying their trade flows but also maintaining strong growth and investment. European stock markets ended up outperforming US exchanges in 2025, rewarding investors who put their trust in our economy. Unemployment is hovering near record lows, and growth is picking up – thanks to high-performing countries such as Spain and Poland. Europe has emerged as a beacon of stability in an uncertain world.
Time and again, the EU has adapted and reinvented itself in the face of crises, leaving it well prepared to navigate a tempestuous geopolitical environment. An export powerhouse, the EU is home to world-class universities and research centres, as well as a vibrant start-up ecosystem. Opinion polls show record levels of public support for the EU and the euro, and global surveys indicate that majorities around the world see the EU as a great power on an equal footing with the US and China.
European stock markets ended up outperforming US exchanges in 2025
They are right to do so. With a $22trn economy, a vast single market of nearly a half-billion people, and plans for another wave of enlargement, Europe’s weight in the world is undeniable. It may be a different kind of superpower, one that prizes values, rules, and multilateralism over sheer might. But its power lies in its commitment to principles and willingness to back its partners and allies, as demonstrated by its status as the biggest source of financial and military assistance to Ukraine.
Europe continues to build bridges in a world of walls. It is the world’s leading trade power, residing at the centre of a vast, ever-expanding network of free-trade agreements. It is also an investment superpower that promotes shared prosperity around the world. As the biggest source of humanitarian aid and development finance, Europe funds everything from global vaccination campaigns to projects to improve water supplies in Amman and Karachi. We do so because we remain committed to the same values that brought us this far. European unification started nearly eight decades ago from the ashes of two world wars. Our parents and grandparents learned from the tragedies and mistakes of that dark era, and we can draw inspiration from their example to shape a better future for ourselves and others around the world. Ours is a society based on inclusion, equality of opportunity, intellectual freedom, peace, and the rule of law.
We know what needs to be done to preserve this way of life. We need even deeper integration, including our capital markets. We need even more large-scale investment in critical infrastructure and strategic capabilities. We need simplification to make the EU more agile and efficient. And we need more win-win partnerships and alliances to diversify our supply chains and open new markets for our goods. Momentum is building in all these areas. European leaders’ minds are focused, and we are determined to capitalise on Europe’s strengths as the world’s underappreciated superpower.

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.

UW–Madison has been named the top volunteer-producing university since 2017.
“Best Value Schools” ranking also jumps 23 spots, placing UW–Madison 24th in the nation.
WSUM rules the airwaves thanks to creative freedom and hard work.
The project ensures that UW–Madison’s efforts at IceCube remain at the forefront of neutrino astronomy for years to come.

articles.title_orig: Indonesia Announces End to “World’s Largest Deforestation Project”
articles.title_zh: Indonesia Announces End to “World’s Largest Deforestation Project”
articles.content_orig:
Global Communications Director
The Government of Indonesia has announced that it will stop any further expansion of the Food and Energy Estates project in Papua and will shift all future development for the project for food and crops for bioenergy to degraded lands – a globally significant win for Indonesia’s nature, the climate, and local communities.
In twin announcements at the Indonesian Sustainability Forum in Jakarta, President Prabowo’s brother Hashim Djojohadikusumo, in his role as Special Envoy for Climate and Energy and the President’s Special Envoy for Multilateralism & International Trade Mari Pangestu said that Indonesia would shift both the rice and sugarcane projects to degraded land.
Mighty Earth Founder and CEO Glenn Hurowitz commented:
“President Prabowo and the Indonesian government have made a globally significant decision for people, nature and climate today by ending deforestation for its food and energy development. This decision renews Indonesia’s leadership in showing how to expand agriculture while protecting nature.”
“Mighty Earth and allies will be closely monitoring implementation, and supporting work with local communities in Papua to heal the damage that’s been done. We are hopeful about the potential of this decision to drive a continued shift to protecting and restoring nature and to sustainable agriculture.”
“This decision creates an opportunity for large-scale investments in achieving President Prabowo’s goal of restoring 12 million hectares of forest, peat, and other ecosystems. It’s a program of truly enormous significance that could provide habitat to endangered species and suck gigatons of carbon out of the atmosphere. We call on all friends of Indonesia to support this program. This decision means that Indonesia can fully achieve its potential to become a nature and climate superpower.”
01:14:00 – Rice Project Announcement by Pak Hashim, Special Envoy of the President for Energy and Climate Change.
03:19:00 – Rice and Energy Project Announcement by Ibu Mari Pangestu, Special Envoy of the President for Multilateralism & International Trade.
Excerpt from President Prabowo’s Special Envoy Hashim Djojohadikusumo speech:
“I’d like to make a major announcement. Now, because of our success in reaching rice self-sufficiency, the Government of Indonesia would like to announce especially by the Minister of Agriculture through me the Special Envoy, that the Ministry of Agriculture and the Government feels at the moment that it does not need to expand the further cultivation of rice in so-called forest areas.
The so-called 2-million-hectare food estate program is a program that we have already achieved without even planting 2 million hectares. We will embark and continue on intensification measures, using new breeds, new seeds, superior breeds of rice and soybeans to achieve that. So, I’d like to again reiterate the fact that the government sees no further need for expanding rice cultivation areas in the so-called forest areas and forest zones that were announced a few years ago…”
Excerpt from President’s Special Envoy Mari Pangestu remarks:
“I just want to repeat a very important message from Pak Hashim this morning…He basically said that because we have been committed Because we have been quite successful meaning that the 2 million hectares that were announced for food production are no longer needed. And he told me he forgot to say it and he asked me to add this message, is that, to, to have increased food and and biofuel production, moving forward, we will be using degraded land…
The missing part of that message is…We have over 12 million hectares of degraded land that can be used, for this, and the minute, and he asked me to say on his behalf that He did discuss this already with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry, and they agreed that any future production of food or biofuel production will be using degraded land, and it is part of the forestry ministry program of afforestation, reforestation, and revegetation.”

articles.title_orig: Amazon kills Alexa’s ability to control Echo speakers’ AUX input
articles.title_zh: Amazon kills Alexa’s ability to control Echo speakers’ AUX input
articles.content_orig:
Amazon has disabled Alexa control of devices plugged into the company’s Echo smart speaker’s AUX port.
Users have reported receiving an email from Amazon this week informing them of the change. “This is a reminder that as of today, voice commands to control your Echo device’s Aux input are no longer available. Requests like ‘Alexa, play from line in” or “Alexa, set aux input’ will no longer work,” an email that Amazon sent reads, according to a screenshot a Reddit user shared this week.
An Amazon spokesperson confirmed the news to Ars Technica today.
Amazon hasn’t made an Echo with a 3.5 mm port in years. The change affects only some older Echo devices: the Echo Plus 2nd Gen (released in 2018), Echo 3rd Gen (released in 2019), Echo Studio 1st Gen (released in 2019), and Echo 4th Gen (released in 2020).
The physical AUX inputs continue to work, so users can still listen to audio from a device connected to an Echo’s 3.5 mm port. They can also continue to use the Alexa app to enable or disable a supporting speaker’s AUX input.
Amazon’s representative also noted that users can still connect a device to their Echo via Bluetooth, which is likely the most common way of connecting third-party devices to Amazon speakers today. The spokesperson said that very few people use voice commands to control audio from a device connected to an Echo’s AUX, which suggests that few users are affected.
Still, it’s frustrating to see a company remove a feature from purchased devices that users may have relied on for years and without a stated reason. Amazon’s representative didn’t answer Ars’ questions about why Amazon removed this Alexa capability or how many users are affected.
“They had the functionality, it’s not like it was a security issue or anything. I cannot understand the reason they’d simply remove a function beyond enshittification,” a Reddit user said in response to the news.
Removing the feature may make it easier for Amazon to maintain Alexa, especially as Amazon puts more resources into improving its AI-powered, subscription-based version of Alexa, Alexa+.
This isn’t the first time Amazon has removed functionality from purchased devices. Last year, it removed users’ ability to block their Echo device from sending voice recordings of commands spoken to Alexa to Amazon. The Echo 4th Gen, Echo Show 15, and Echo Show 10 supported the capability.

articles.title_orig: Lawsuit Targets Utah Oil Highway Threatening World-Renowned Nine Mile Canyon
articles.title_zh: Lawsuit Targets Utah Oil Highway Threatening World-Renowned Nine Mile Canyon
articles.content_orig:
For Immediate Release,
                 
                
                October 6, 2026
Grant Stevens, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, (319) 427-0260, [email protected] Mike Hansen, Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, (801) 916-2491, [email protected] Deeda Seed, Center for Biological Diversity, (801) 803-9892, [email protected]
Lawsuit Targets Utah Oil Highway Threatening World-Renowned Nine Mile Canyon
Construction to Demolish 100-Foot-Tall Canyon Walls, Damage Native Rock Imagery, Utah History
SALT LAKE CITY— The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, and Center for Biological Diversity today sued the Trump administration’s Bureau of Land Management for approving construction of a hydrocarbon highway through Utah’s scenic, culturally and historically significant Gate Canyon in eastern Utah.
The project to straighten 6 miles of what is currently a scenic, winding, gravel road through Gate Canyon involves the blasting and destruction of 100-foot tall canyon walls, damaging Native rock imagery, Utah pioneer history and habitat for threatened wildlife.
“This lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s disgraceful plan to transform a quiet backcountry road into a highway clogged with speeding oil tanker trucks,” said Deeda Seed, senior Utah campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Blasting through Gate Canyon’s walls will be a disaster for nearby animals, including threatened Mexican spotted owls. We’re going to court to protect this irreplaceable cultural treasure and the animals calling it home.”
Gate Canyon is located in Utah’s West Tavaputs Plateau region, between the towns of Myton and Wellington. It feeds into Nine Mile Canyon — a world-renowned archaeological area that contains more than 10,000 unique, irreplaceable cultural, historical and archaeological resources. The proposed route of the highway, designed to accommodate 70-foot oil tankers, cuts directly through the rugged landscape and will fundamentally alter the character of Gate Canyon.
“In the words of Joni Mitchell, the BLM has approved the 'paving of paradise.' But instead of putting in a parking lot, the BLM has given its OK to the building of a highway to carry crude oil from the Uinta Basin to Carbon County,” said J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition. “It's like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum."
Today’s lawsuit challenges the BLM’s rushed and behind-closed-doors environmental review for failing to disclose or analyze the threats of increased traffic and canyon blasting on wildlife, the area’s rock imagery, historic axle grease inscriptions and scenery, and for failing to consider alternative, less damaging routes.
The BLM also ignored its own resource management plans that require protecting the area’s cultural and scenic values and violated the federal National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The bureau failed to consider the project’s threats to Mexican spotted owls , despite the fact that the cliffs near the proposed blasting areas are identified as potential owl habitat.
“The BLM knew that prior versions of this same proposal were extremely controversial and faced fierce public headwinds,” said Landon Newell, staff attorney with the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance. “This time around, instead of facing the public, they hid their decision and rushed their analysis and approval, all under the guise of Trump’s “Energy Dominance” agenda.”
The project , known as the “Wells Draw Road Amendment – Gate Canyon,” was proposed by Duchesne County and approved by the BLM on April 28, 2026. It is intended to provide an alternative route for transporting oil out of the Uinta Basin. The current backcountry road would be transformed to accommodate 70-foot oil tanker trucks traveling to the oil fields and transloading facilities in Carbon County, Utah. If the destruction of Gate Canyon moves forward, as many as 1,000 vehicles could pass through each day — the equivalent of “ [a] tanker truck every 7 minutes ,” according to news reports.
This marks the third attempt by Duchesne County to destroy Gate Canyon. In 2015 and 2022 , the BLM received similar applications to realign Gate Canyon Road, but those projects were abandoned amid significant public opposition . The BLM quietly posted the latest iteration of the project in March 2026 without issuing public notice or opening a formal comment period. After learning of the project, conservation groups quickly requested that the BLM allow for public participation opportunities in the decision-making process. The agency denied those requests and quickly approved the project in late April.
Nine Mile Canyon is often referred to as “the world’s longest art gallery” because of its extensive collection of rock imagery and archeological sites. Previous BLM studies describe the area as containing “a significant and high density of historic, cultural, and archeological sites joined together in several overlapping historic landscapes” and saying it “is known to contain the country’s highest concentration of rock imagery panels, remnants of the prehistoric Archaic, Fremont, and Ute cultures…The rock structural remains of Fremont homes, granaries, and ‘forts’ are more visible in Nine Mile Canyon than almost anywhere in the Fremont cultural area.”
The Center for Biological Diversity is a national, nonprofit conservation organization with more than 1.8 million members and online activists dedicated to the protection of endangered species and wild places.

articles.title_orig: U.S. military to conduct first firing squad execution since World War II
articles.title_zh: U.S. military to conduct first firing squad execution since World War II
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump has ordered the rare use of a firing squad for the execution of a former army major who killed 13 people in Texas in 2009.
Former army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan’s method of execution was approved by the president at the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth , Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.
Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 , killing 12 active-duty but unarmed ⁠soldiers and a retired serviceman and injured 32 people. He was sentenced to death after being convicted on 45 counts of premeditated murder in 2013 for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to deploy to Afghanistan . Prosecutors said he was motivated by unwillingness to be sent to Afghanistan and the shooting was in retaliation for America’s wars in the Muslim world.
Hasan was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police upon his arrest.
Parnell said the "judgment day for Hasan has finally come" and that the date and place of his death would be set by the secretary of the army.
Death by firing squad was one of the forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently ⁠added to the list of permissible methods of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution. The number ​of federal ⁠execution options was expanded in part because of ‌increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which had also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.
Hasan is one of four military inmates awaiting execution, which requires approval from the president and an appellate review.
Hasan's military execution is different from the majority of executions, which are legal in 27 states of America.
Execution by firing squad is rare in the country, with the latest being carried out last year in South Carolina .
In 2024, the South Carolina Supreme Court had ruled that firing squad, lethal injection and electric chair were all legal methods of execution. The court noted the firing squad was not cruel because a prisoner would not suffer longer than 15 seconds.
Brad Sigmon became the first person in the state to be executed by firing squad and the first across the country in 15 years. Mikal Mahdi was executed in a similar way on 11 April.
In all, at least six people have been executed by firing squad since the country reinstated the death penalty in 1977.
Since 1608, at least 145 civilian prisoners have been executed by shooting, nearly all in the state of Utah, according to the Associated Press.
Hasan will be the first person to face a military firing squad since the end of World War II. His will also be the first ⁠military execution, by any method, since 1961.
The last military execution, the Death Penalty Information Center said, was done by hanging, while the last-known execution by a military firing squad was likely carried out "by musketry" in November 1945.
Trump, a supporter of the federal death penalty, reinstated the execution method on his first day back as president in January 2025.
At least five states have firing ​squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information ‌Center. The Utah Supreme Court halted the scheduled 5 September 2025 firing-squad execution of death-row inmate Ralph Menzies.
Trump's approval for Hasan’s execution comes as plans by Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 ‌years went awry last week.
Prison personnel botched an attempt to ‌administer a lethal injection, leaving Christa Pike alive but unconscious and hospitalised on life support.
Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners would face in establishing ⁠a sound intravenous line.
"There’s nothing Donald Trump loves ‌more than the power to kill," Death Penalty Action, a campaign group opposed to capital punishment, said, pointing out that he oversaw more executions during his first term than any president since Franklin D Roosevelt. “Truly, this is just another distraction and a ploy to stem his record-low approval ratings."

articles.title_orig: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.title_zh: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.content_orig:
It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?
T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”
I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.
Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan.
Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh.
And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”.
For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come.
Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.”
While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque.
It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs.
It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer.
Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.”
The prettiness of Le Butter’s packaging has naturally made it a social media hit, which Leo describes as a double-edged sword. “Obviously, I’m grateful,” he says. “But it can also be overwhelming. The aim of the shop is to educate people beyond supermarket butter, and to serve the locals as well as the tourists. We can only do our best.”
This fetishisation of butter is still quite divisive. “When it comes to food styling, some of what they do looks cool,” says Seb Myers of the restaurant Planque in east London. “But when you see a mound of butter – all that extravagance for the sake of a photo? I’m quite squirrelly with food. Waste is my big thing.”
In restaurants, I’ve lost count of the time I’ve been served butter shaped into little salted coins or whipped into something dippable. Bread and butter are still one of the most valued moments in a good meal. And as Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential, “If you eat at any good restaurant, assume you’ve eaten a stick of butter.”
“That’s partly because it starts the meal,” says Myers, who takes his butter pretty seriously. “If someone serves you an ice-cold pat of butter, you know you’re not in for a good time”. His restaurant is a play on Parisian bistronomy, so “it’s in almost every dish”. They use Beillevaire butter demi-sel sprinkled with flakes, sliced and well tempered. He keeps it in “a cheese fridge for a week to slow-mature it”. For cooking, it’s Douceur de France (they get through 10kg a week in cooking alone).
Pravin Nayar runs Castle Farm restaurant in Somerset, and makes his own: “We like butter to be the hero product when we do supper clubs.” The key, he says, is how you serve it: room temperature, sprinkled with salt. “The way I see it, bread is just a spoon for butter.”
R emember when butter was considered bad? After all those anti-saturated fat health campaigns, consumption hit a historic low by the late 1990s, with the average Brit consuming just 2kg a year. The perception around it seems to have shifted, although with 50% saturated fat – and I say this with love – butter is not exactly a superfood.
“The heart-health advice hasn’t changed,” says Tracy Parker, a registered dietitian and an adviser for the British Heart Foundation. “If you’ve got high cholesterol, or your diet already leans heavily on saturated fat – think fatty meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits – then you should probably reconsider how much you’re eating and whether you could swap it for something like olive, avocado or nut oil.” Butter is fine in moderation, though. “A light scrape on your morning toast, and thinking about everything else you eat – you’re probably OK,” she says.
So why the cultural rehabilitation of butter in a health-fad-mad 2026? Parker thinks it has become tangled up with the anti-ultraprocessed-food movement. “UPFs have been linked to poor health including obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease,” she says. Whereas butter is seen as a preindustrial, farm-adjacent product. “People view butter as a natural food

articles.title_orig: UVA index ranks US second in world’s most capitalist countries
articles.title_zh: UVA index ranks US second in world’s most capitalist countries
articles.content_orig:
Three years in the making, the Global Capitalism Index – the product of experts at UVA’s Darden School of Business and Karsh Institute of Democracy – helps people better understand how capitalist conditions relate to democracy, corruption, human well-being and inequality within a country. (Illustration by Meredith Michael Smith, University Communications)
Switzerland is the most capitalistic country in the world, with the United States coming in a close second, according to a first-ever global index and data set from the University of Virginia.
Three years in the making , the Global Capitalism Index is the product of experts at UVA’s Darden School of Business and Karsh Institute of Democracy. The index scores 161 countries across eight measures of capitalism, including ease of business formation and the flow of goods to and from the country.
Experts involved in creating the index said the data show promise for understanding how capitalist conditions relate to democracy, corruption, human well-being, and inequality within a country. A team of researchers led by the Karsh Institute of Democracy’s Democracy and Capitalism Lab and UVA Darden’s Institute for Business in Society assembled the data to help define and measure capitalism worldwide.
The index uses figures compiled from 2009 to 2025 and is designed to be updated.
“Understanding the conditions that allow democratic self-government to thrive requires us to examine the economic systems in which people and institutions operate,” said Melody Barnes, executive director of the Karsh Institute of Democracy. “The Global Capitalism Index gives researchers a rigorous new tool for examining how different forms of capitalism relate to democratic institutions, individual well-being, inequality and other dimensions of democratic life.”
Although there is a large body of research on the concept and function of democracy, there is little on capitalism, the researchers wrote.
“For decades, scholars, policymakers and the public have lacked a rigorous, quantitative framework for defining and measuring capitalism,” the index authors wrote in an executive summary. “Even capitalism’s intellectual champions – Adam Smith, Joseph Schumpeter, Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman and others – produced widely varied definitions of the concept. …There is a substantial body of literature defining democracy, but scholarly efforts to define and measure capitalism have been difficult and fractured.”
Interactive world map showing Global Capitalism Index scores.
            Higher-ranked countries are shown in darker blue.
            Use the Tab key to explore countries on the map, or view the
            complete data table below.
Under the index’s 100-point scale, the top-ranked country was Switzerland at 96.6, followed by the U.S. at 95, Hong Kong at 94.5 and Canada at 93.8.
From the bottom rankings, Venezuela scored 8.9; Libya, 21.8; Chad, 24.1; and Mauritania, 24.2.
“If you ask anyone what capitalism is, the answers are all different, and that makes it hard to argue about the validity or value of it,” said Scott Miller, an assistant business professor at the Darden School, director of the Democracy and Capitalism Lab and lead author on the project. “We concluded that this word – capitalism – matters to everyone, so it matters to define it and measure how it really works across the globe.”
Looking at different sectors of capitalism in a country adds nuance and insight into its economy and culture, index authors said. For example, Seychelles and China rank 50th and 33rd, respectively, and Nordic countries rank highly overall, even though they are associated with high levels of social support.
Here are the U.S. rankings listed in the index:
In addition to comparing countries, the index also examines different forms of capitalism. Rather than a monolithic economic model, the index examines capitalism in four categories:
“For individual countries, the index makes it much easier to identify what conditions are conducive to capitalism and which are not,” Miller said. “Using China as an example, we can see in sharper relief the profile and shape of the underlying economy, including surprisingly strong business conditions, but increasingly restricted flow of goods and capital.”
Assistant Editor, UVA Today Office of University Communications

articles.title_orig: Some sugar-free Starbucks drinks have as much sugar as a Kit Kat bar, lawsuit says
articles.title_zh: Some sugar-free Starbucks drinks have as much sugar as a Kit Kat bar, lawsuit says
articles.content_orig:
A consumer lawsuit is accusing Starbucks of adding sugar, sometimes as much as that in a Kit Kat bar, to drinks marketed as sugar free.
The products in question include hot and iced protein lattes and protein matcha beverages in vanilla and caramel flavors. According to the federal lawsuit filed Friday, these drinks contain 13 to 21 grams of sugar per serving.
“No reasonable person” would expect something labeled “sugar-free” to contain that much sugar, the lawsuit contends.
“This case is about false and misleading product names. It is not about missing nutritional information,” according to the lawsuit.
Starbucks denied misleading consumers with its menu in a statement to NBC News on Tuesday.  The international coffee chain said it has “consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices, and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter.”
Hagens Berman filed the suit on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks’ sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York and Washington, The Associated Press reported .
“Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant,” Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm, told the AP.
Seattle-based Starbucks said the sugar in its protein drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk it uses. The company said it doesn’t add sugar to the drinks and it uses sugar-free syrup for flavoring.
On Starbucks’ website Monday, the drinks were marketed as “sugar-free,” but the company also stated the amount of sugar in each beverage and that they were made without added sugar .
The lawsuit seeks damages on behalf of U.S. consumers who bought the drinks. It also wants the court to order Starbucks to stop using the label “sugar-free” on products that contain sugar.
Alicia Victoria Lozano is a California-based reporter for NBC News focusing on climate change, wildfires and the changing politics of drug laws.
Insiya Gandhi is an Assignment Editor based in New York.

articles.title_orig: Novavax, Moderna stocks fall after WHO calls plague risk 'low'
articles.title_zh: Novavax, Moderna stocks fall after WHO calls plague risk 'low'
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Novavax stock ( NVAX ) fell on Tuesday after a World Health Organization (WHO) spokesperson told reporters that there was a "low" risk of a plague epidemic, after a 28-year-old woman who worked in a Russian anti-plague laboratory died last week .
Shares of Novavax fell nearly 10%, pulling back from a 20% gain the day before that was fueled by concerns about a potential outbreak. Moderna ( MRNA ) stock fell 7%, giving back all its gains from Monday. BioNTech ( BNTX ) fell 2%, while Pfizer ( PFE ) was little changed.
A worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East died of "pneumonia of undetermined" origin last week, raising concerns about a potential global health scare.
The WHO is investigating whether the death was due to pneumonic plague, a highly contagious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Pneumonic plague is curable with antibiotics if caught early, but it can be fatal within 24 hours of onset if left untreated, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said.
Lindmeier noted that Shipilova's workplace was "an institute that studies dangerous pathogens, including plague, in a part of Siberia where plague occurs naturally in wild animals."
Lindemeier said WHO had identified and tested the worker's contacts and did not detect plague or pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases.
"None to date have shown symptoms of illness," he said of the contacts.
WHO "estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region," Lindmeier added.
US officials have called on Russia to be more transparent about the incident. Russian authorities reportedly put one hospital facility and dozens ‌of people under quarantine.
"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more ‌information with the ⁠world," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday. "We're watching it very closely, hour by ⁠hour."

articles.title_orig: ‘Raging desire for revenge’: How does the Arab world remember Hamas’s October 7 invasion?
articles.title_zh: ‘Raging desire for revenge’: How does the Arab world remember Hamas’s October 7 invasion?
articles.content_orig:
Three years after Hamas's October 7 invasion of Israel, Arab media coverage of the anniversary has focused heavily on the devastation in Gaza, often making little or no mention of the Israeli civilians killed in the attack that sparked the war and sometimes going as far as to celebrate it.
The Jerusalem Post has not identified a statement from an Arab leader expressing sympathy for Israeli victims of the October 7 attack as of Tuesday. However, Hamas shared a condemnation of the statement issued by UN Secretary-General António Guterres on the invasion.
Hamas has continued to deny targeting civilians, carrying out sexual assaults and mistreating hostages in captivity, claiming that investigations had disproved the allegations. However, a UN mission that visited Israel concluded that there were reasonable grounds to believe conflict-related sexual violence occurred during the October 7 massacre and that there was clear and convincing information that hostages had been subjected to sexual violence in captivity.
Former hostages have also repeatedly described the torture, starvation, and sexual violence they experienced while they were held against their will in Gaza.
Hamas demanded Guterres retract his statement, which acknowledged Hamas and other Palestinian terrorists “brutally” killed more than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals, deliberately targeted civilians and sexually assaulted and tortured hostages in captivity.
Though Guterres expressed sympathy for the victims of October 7, his statement also addressed the “untold suffering on Palestinians in Gaza” and insisted that both Hamas and Israel need to enter the next stage of the ceasefire agreement.
The Egyptian state-owned Maspero marked the anniversary of Hamas’s October 7 attack using the terrorist group’s name for the assault, publishing an article titled “New details emerge about the Al-Aqsa Flood... and the region’s involvement in a chaos plot” that featured exclusively Palestinian and Egyptian professors.
The article failed to share the number of Israelis killed during the “crushing blow,” instead reporting only that Hamas was able to “occupy the settlements located in the envelope” and kill “hundreds of soldiers and officers of the Zionist entity.”
Unmentioned in the report was that more than 800 of those killed on October 7 were civilians. The youngest known victim was Naama Abu Rashed, a Bedouin-Israeli newborn who died just 14 hours after she was delivered by emergency Cesarean section after her pregnant mother was shot in the stomach while being driven to hospital.
“Events did not end with the clashes of October 7th. As expected, they escalated into a war of extermination waged by the Zionist entity against the Gaza Strip, during which approximately 74,000 Palestinians were killed, and about 100,000 others were wounded,” the report continued.
“Around 90 percent of Gaza's buildings were destroyed, and its infrastructure was almost completely obliterated. The war did not stop at Gaza; it extended to wars against Lebanon and then against Iran, leading to subsequent changes in the map of the Middle East.”
The state media did not mention Hezbollah’s attacks on October 8, 2023, which led to the war on the northern front, instead focusing on the view of Dr. Emad Mohsen, who alleged Israel “unleashed the killing machine accompanied by intense hatred, loathing, and a raging desire for revenge,” which resulted in “genocide, famine, crimes against humanity, and the most heinous forms of violent behavior on a human level.”
“Above all, the true face of Zionist extremism, its expansionist desire, its thirst for Palestinian and Arab blood, its call for displacement, genocide, murder, settlement, and the undermining of the Palestinian dream of freedom and national independence, was revealed,” the paper published.
Al Ghad , the first independent daily Arabic newspaper in Jordan, also failed to mention the specific number of victims in its article on the massacre, instead focusing on Israel closing the crossing from Gaza and the West Bank for two days.
“On the morning of October 7, 2023, Hamas surprised Israel with an unprecedented attack on 11 military bases and 22 settlements along the Gaza Strip, resulting in the death, injury, and capture of hundreds of Israelis,” it reported on Sunday, adding that the explanation that Hamas argued it committed the attack "to end the unjust siege on Gaza and to thwart Israel's plans to liquidate the Palestinian cause and impose its sovereignty over the Al-Aqsa Mosque."
It also focused on the civilian deaths in Gaza, relying on figures by the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, which doesn’t distinguish between combatant and civilian deaths.
The independent Lebanese news website Janoubia published a practical analysis of the threats facing Israel and its military successes since October 7 in an article titled “8 dangers threatening Israel on ‘October 7th!’”
Although the article referred to the attack as “ Operation Al-Aqsa Flood ” and did not mention its victims, it focused on Israel’s security situation and acknowledged several of the IDF’s achievements. It also mentioned the displacement of Israelis from communities near the northern and southern borders following the attacks, an aspect of the war that has received relatively little attention in much international media coverage.
Asharq Al-Awsat , a Saudi-owned media group headquartered in London, published an article stressing that assassinated Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had warned Israel in 2022 that Hamas would respond if Israel continued “attacks” on Al-Aqsa Mosque and Jerusalem.
The article attributed the launch of “Operation Al-Aqsa Flood” on October 7, 2023, to Israeli actions and focused on whether Hamas had achieved its objectives. It noted that Sinwar had promised to empty Israel’s prisons of security prisoners, thousands of whom were released as part of hostage-prisoner exchanges during the war.
The article also acknowledged Israel’s “unprecedented” success in assassinating Hamas’s leadership, while accusing the IDF of conducting “an indiscriminate bombing campaign across the Gaza Strip” and, citing a UN committee, claiming that “Israel has sought to wipe out Gaza through a genocide operation.”
At the same time, Asharq Al-Awsat quoted Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim criticizing Sinwar, saying that “popular criticism of Sinwar and anger over his ill-considered decision continue,” alongside the suffering of Gaza residents who lost their homes and property. Ibrahim added that Palestinians outside Gaza might support Sinwar’s actions because they had not experienced the same destruction, killing, and displacement.
Another recurring theme in Arab coverage was whether Netanyahu had received advance warnings of the attack from Arab states, shifting attention from Hamas’s actions to alleged Israeli intelligence and political failures. Haaretz first reported that Netanyahu denied receiving advance warning from the United Arab Emirates, while The Wall Street Journal later reported that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had warned Netanyahu of Hamas’s plans. Netanyahu has denied receiving such a warning.

articles.title_orig: Jim Bakker, who lost his ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire in sex and money scandals, dies at 86
articles.title_zh: Jim Bakker, who lost his ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire in sex and money scandals, dies at 86
articles.content_orig:
Jim Bakker, the charismatic evangelical preacher who built a Christian television empire, only to see it collapse in scandal, recrimination and prison, died Monday, his wife said.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” his second wife, Lori Bakker, said on the Facebook page of his most recent TV show , “The Jim Bakker Show.” She did not disclose a cause of death.
Bakker’s son, Jay Bakker, who became a prominent evangelist in his own right with a much more liberal view of Christianity than his father’s, confirmed the death in his own Facebook post .
“We had a very complicated relationship and he was also my father and a grandfather and I need to mourn in my own time,” he wrote.
Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and his flamboyant first wife, Tammy Faye, was born in International Falls, Minnesota, but they embraced the South when they started a puppet show on a Virginia TV station in the 1970s. It soon turned into a high-energy, Southern-flavored talk show called “The PTL Club” on cable, attracting some of the biggest celebrities of the 1980s to tell their stories of having been “born again.”
Bakker launched the first Christian satellite network to beam his upbeat message — “God loves you. He really does” — into homes across the country and around the world.
Along the way, they became known in the secular world for their easy tears, his welcoming but often strict message and her neon personality — and makeup.
Their ministry grew rapidly, and operating out of its new base in Fort Mill, South Carolina, along the North Carolina line, they built a multimillion-dollar empire complete with one of the world’s largest theme parks, Heritage USA, on the small donations of hundreds of thousands of believers, some of whom pledged their life savings to them.
But PTL — short, variously, for Praise the Lord or People That Love — collapsed in 1987, when The Charlotte Observer reported that it had paid more than $250,000 to Jessica Hahn, a church secretary with whom Bakker had a one-time tryst years earlier. Bakker confirmed the encounter to the Observer but said he had been “wickedly manipulated by treacherous former friends and then colleagues who victimized me with the aid of a female confederate.”
Further reporting disclosed lavish spending on the Bakkers’ behalf, including an air-conditioned doghouse at their lakefront home and gold-plated bathroom fixtures. The Bakkers resigned from PTL, and in 1989, Bakker was convicted of fraud and conspiracy and sentenced to 45 years in prison; he served just less than five years before he was paroled.
Tammy Bakker resolutely stood by him for several years, but in 1992 she filed for divorce. She married the man whose contracting service built much of Heritage USA — and who provided most of the money to pay Hahn — and slowly rebuilt her life as a Christian TV personality who knowingly winked at her own image for secular audiences . She died of cancer in 2007.
Bakker returned to ministry after his prison term and in 2003 launched “The Jim Bakker Show” with Lori Bakker, whom he had married in 1998.
Bakker’s message was far different this time — apocalyptic and dismissive of the prosperity theology that brought him to fame. The show focused on a survivalist message, and Bakker built a new business based on promoting unregulated supplements. In 2021, he and his church settled a lawsuit from the state of Missouri that accused him of falsely claiming a health supplement called Silver Solution could cure Covid.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” Lori Bakker said Monday night in announcing his death.
Alex Johnson has been a reporter and editor for NBC News since 2000. He previously worked for The Charlotte Observer, Congressional Quarterly, Knight-Ridder and The Washington Post.

articles.title_orig: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
articles.title_zh: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
articles.content_orig:
British Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers.
The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub.
British Airways said the 106 business-class suites, with sliding doors, will take up the entirety of the A380's upper deck.
Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips.
British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines , last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in a recent interview that customers are seeking high-end options on long flights, like its Perth-London nonstop.
"There is absolutely a customer who wants this and is prepared to pay a premium for it," she said.
Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase.
The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights.
Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification.
British Airways' overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021.

articles.title_orig: Tampa General spine program first in world to receive accreditation
articles.title_zh: Tampa General spine program first in world to receive accreditation
articles.content_orig:
Tampa General Hospital’s Neuro Spine Program has earned a Center of Excellence designation from the Surgical Review Corp., becoming the first program in the world to receive the organization’s accreditation in that field, the hospital says.
TGH announced the new accreditation Tuesday alongside individual distinctions for four surgeons. Dr. Puya Alikhani earned SRC’s Master Surgeon designation in Neuro Spine Surgery — another worldwide first, according to TGH. Drs. Patrick Kim, Erik Hayman and Alexander Haas were named Surgeons of Excellence.
The SRC is an independent, nonprofit patient safety organization formed in 2003 that develops and administers global accreditation programs for hospitals, outpatient facilities and medical professionals, according to its website.
The accreditation process includes an on-site assessment and a review of surgical case volume, facility resources, clinical protocols, patient education and ongoing quality improvement, the announcement says. The hospital says the assessment also provided recommendations for improving care.
The TGH program works with USF Health spine surgeons to treat conditions ranging from degenerative neck and lower-back disorders to spinal deformities, tumors and infections. Its services include surgical and nonsurgical treatment for scoliosis.
“This designation provides patients and families with added confidence that they are choosing a spine program that meets the highest standards of quality, safety and outcomes,” Luke Straus, vice president of the TGH Neurosciences and Orthopedic Institutes, says in the release.
Tampa General is a nonprofit academic health system with 1,530 beds across its network, according to the release.
Anastasia Dawson is a Tampa Bay reporter at the Business Observer. Before joining Observer Media Group, the award-winning journalist worked at the Tampa Bay Times and the Tampa Tribune. She lives in Plant City with her shih tzu, Alfie.

articles.title_orig: Google could soon solve Pixel's biggest face unlock flaw
articles.title_zh: Google could soon solve Pixel's biggest face unlock flaw
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Google’s modern face unlock on recent Pixel flagships is Class 3 biometric certified, but as anyone who has tried unlocking their phone in a dim bedroom knows, it is practically useless once the lights go down. That shortcoming has long fueled anticipation around Google’s secretive Project Toscana , an effort to overhaul facial authentication across Pixel devices, Chromebooks, and presumably Googlebooks by extension. Now, new code discovered in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 reveals that Google is actively building a “Face Active Illumination” system to help solve face unlock’s low-light authentication woes.
You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.
We’ve spotted several clues in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 suggesting Google is working on a “Face Active Illumination” feature for Pixel devices, at least, which could make face authentication more reliable in low-light conditions. The code points to dedicated toggles for activating the feature, controlling its brightness, and specifying when it should be allowed to activate, but it doesn’t reveal exactly which hardware provides the illumination.
While we managed to activate the feature, we could only get an incomplete and seemingly empty UI to appear at this stage. Strings within the app (other than the “Do Not Disturb” text) are also obfuscated, so there’s still a fair bit of mystery around this feature, how it would work, and what it could even be called for its final marketing name.
From the UI, we can infer that the “Face Active Illumination” feature is within the Face Unlock settings and may offer three brightness levels via a slider. When read with the code, the toggles could let users choose whether illumination will be used in dark environments (maybe referring to dark mode?), during bedtime hours, during Do Not Disturb, and while driving.
It’s unclear whether Face Active Illumination uses IR technology, as previously spotted under Project Toscana, or is merely ramping up screen brightness to throw more light on your face for easier face unlock. The presence of toggles doesn’t instill confidence for the former, as users wouldn’t need granular control over an IR-based system, much like we see (or quite literally, don’t see) with Face ID on the iPhone. It is thus likely to be the latter, as the toggles would allow users to avoid flashbanging themselves with their phone display in certain low-light situations.
Google hasn’t announced any details about Face Active Illumination or Project Toscana, and there’s a fair chance the two aren’t related. We’ll keep you updated when we learn more details about either.

articles.title_orig: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes | US midterm elections 2026
articles.title_zh: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes | US midterm elections 2026
articles.content_orig:
Polls show GOP candidates trailing Democrats in Senate races, and Republicans also struggling in House contests
Thirty days remain until the midterm elections, and Donald Trump and his Republican allies are pulling out all the stops to maintain control of Congress.
Super Pacs aligned with the GOP have already spent hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising and voter outreach in races expected to decide the majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, and plan to spend even more before the election is over. The president, Vice-President JD Vance, and other top Republicans are fanning out across the country to stump for vulnerable lawmakers.
So far, there are no signs the money or the rallies have improved what appears to be a grim state of affairs for Republicans , less than two years after their resounding victories in the 2024 election. Recently released polls continue to show the party’s candidates trailing their Democratic challengers in the Senate races that will decide the majority and control of the chamber.
“Candidate quality is beating gobs of Republican money,” the Senate’s Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, quipped over the weekend, when the New York Times released the latest in a series of closely watched polls that confirmed the momentum behind their bid to retake the Senate.
The surveys, conducted with Siena University, found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas – all states Trump won by double digits two years ago. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years , the party’s candidate Adam Hamilton was neck-and-neck with the Republican senator Roger Marshall, while in Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is narrowly trailing the Republican candidate, Ashley Hinson. Democratic candidates for governor were also leading in many traditionally Republican states, the Times and Siena found .
“If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races [would] go blue,” Briscoe Cain, a Republican state representative in Texas wrote on X Monday. The Democrats’ Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa were both leading in the Times and Siena survey.
“Republican voters feel too comfortable and are not as intense about this election as they should be. We have more voters than the left in Texas, but we have to vote,” Cain added.
Last Friday, the news outlet Semafor reported that the Senate Leadership Fund, a major GOP Super Pac, planned to pull money from the campaign of its candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, in favor of upping support for Marshall in Kansas. No Democrat has won a US Senate election in North Carolina since 2008, but Whatley has trailed in polls for months. Democrats need to win at least four seats in the chamber to regain the majority they lost in the 2024 election.
The situation for Democrats appears to be similarly positive in their campaign to retake the House, which Republicans control only narrowly. A CBS News and YouGov poll released on Sunday found Democrats with a nine percentage point lead on the generic ballot, an important indicator of voter intention in congressional races.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday found Trump’s approval ratings remained at the lowest point of his career, with only 32% of adult respondents approving of his performance as president. Independent voters – whose views often make the difference in close races – planned to back Democrats by a 16-percentage-point margin, though many remained undecided.
The president’s poor marks are believed to be a major cause of the Republican candidates’ struggles nationwide, but are far from the only one. Discontent over the state of the economy – particularly the price of gasoline and other consumer staples – is another reason, as is the on-again, off-again conflict with Iran, and concern over Trump’s hardline approach to enforcing immigration laws.
Republicans maintain they have avenues to victory in both chambers of Congress. Eight House Republicans represent districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, as opposed to 22 House Democrats representing districts Trump won – a number that has grown larger thanks to the unprecedented redistricting war Trump instigated. Many polls show voters have an unfavorable perception of the Democratic party, though views of Republicans are similarly negative. And despite strong fundraising by some Democratic candidates, Republicans and groups allied with their agenda have an edge in cash to spend on this election.
It may not be enough to halt the disintegration that appears to be occurring in the coalition that elected Trump two years ago. Only 26% of Hispanic voters – who swung towards Trump after years of leaning Democratic – plan to vote for Republicans this year, while 52% prefer the Democrats, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
“We’ve been seeing among Latino voters, as we’ve been seeing kind of in the electorate as a whole, a real strong rejection of the Trump administration, and that has inflated into an increase in support for Democratic candidates,” said Maria Isabel Di Franco Quinonez, a senior research director at Equis Research, a progressive firm that focuses on the community.
Should the trend hold, it could bode well for Democrats’ hopes in states and districts with large Latino populations. The effect may be pronounced in Texas, where the Republican leaders drew new congressional maps to favor their candidates, but only if Latino voters continue voting the way they did in 2024.
“If we see those levels continue to rise and see those districts look more like the kinds of support levels for Democrats that we had seen back in 2018, then that would result in maybe Republicans get one more seat after redrawing all the lines, as opposed to getting four or five more seats,” Quinonez said.
